techniques.name: Coefficient Magnitudes (in Linear Models)
techniques.description: Coefficient Magnitudes explains a linear model by reading its fitted coefficients. Each coefficient shows how much the prediction changes when its feature rises by one unit while every other feature stays fixed, and its sign gives the direction. Because a coefficient's size depends on the units of its feature, the features are first put on a common scale, for example by standardising them or by multiplying each coefficient by its feature's standard deviation. The features with the largest scaled coefficients are then read as having the strongest influence on the model's predictions. This gives a global view of the model without needing a separate explanation method.

example_use_cases.description: An estate agency's data team standardises the inputs of a linear house-price model, then ranks the absolute coefficients to show valuers which property attributes move the estimate most. Valuers check that the signs match their experience, for example that more floor area raises the price, before the model guides asking prices.

A lender's model-risk team documents a linear credit-scoring model for its regulator by publishing the standardised coefficient of every input. The reviewer can read off the direction and relative weight of each input without a separate explanation tool, and can query any input that carries more weight than policy allows.

A public health analyst fits a logistic regression to predict emergency readmission and reports standardised coefficients to clinicians, who see which patient characteristics push the predicted risk up or down. The analyst refits on resamples first, to check that the large coefficients keep their sign.

limitations.description: Raw magnitudes have output-per-input units and cannot be ranked across differently scaled variables. Express comparable input changes explicitly; changing metres to centimetres makes the corresponding coefficient smaller for the same predictions.

Coefficients concern the encoded model inputs while other inputs are held fixed. If the model includes transformed variables or interactions, inspecting one coefficient does not give the whole effect of changing an original variable.

Correlated predictors can have unstable or shared coefficients even when predictions change little. Scaling does not remove this problem, and regularisation can change which correlated feature receives a large weight.

Each coefficient is conditional on the other features in the model. A feature can have a negative coefficient while rising with the outcome on its own, so a coefficient read in isolation can mislead about the feature's plain relationship to the outcome.

A coefficient is a conditional association in the fitted model, not a causal effect. Its magnitude alone also does not give a particular applicant's contribution, which depends on that applicant's feature values.

techniques.name: DeepLIFT
techniques.description: DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures) explains a single prediction of a neural network by dividing the difference between the model's output and its output on a reference input among the input features. The reference is a neutral input chosen for the problem, such as an all-zero image or a blurred copy of the input. The method measures how far each neuron's activation is from its value on the reference, then passes those differences backwards through the layers in one pass, applying a rule for each layer type. A plain gradient (the rate of change of the output with respect to an input) is zero where the output has levelled off, but DeepLIFT can still assign credit there. The scores add up to the output difference and mean something only relative to the reference chosen.

example_use_cases.description: A genomics group training a neural network to predict where a regulatory protein binds DNA computes DeepLIFT scores for each predicted binding region against a reference sequence with background base frequencies. They read off which short stretches of bases carry the score, compare them with known binding motifs, and decide whether the model has learned real regulatory sequence before using it to prioritise experiments.

A hospital imaging team is investigating a chest X-ray classifier that flags healthy patients as abnormal. For the false positives it computes DeepLIFT scores against a blurred copy of each image and checks whether the weight sits on the image border, where scanner labels are printed, rather than on lung tissue. It then decides whether to mask the labels and retrain.

A regional geohazard agency uses a neural network to rate landslide susceptibility from terrain, rainfall and land-cover layers. For a slope the model rates as high risk, DeepLIFT scores show which input layers drove the rating, and the agency compares them with the field investigation report before using the map for planning.

A lender's credit team sends each declined applicant a short statement of the factors that most lowered their score. For its neural network scorer it computes DeepLIFT scores against a documented reference applicant, the median approved applicant, and the statement lists the factors with the largest negative scores, which are the ones that pulled this score below the reference.

limitations.description: Every score is relative to a reference input, and the choice changes the picture. In the original paper an all-zero reference on CIFAR-10 images highlighted hard-to-interpret background pixels, while a blurred copy of the image highlighted object outlines. State the reference used and repeat the analysis with at least one alternative before drawing conclusions.

The Captum implementation supports only the Rescale rule, which can give all the credit to one of two inputs that jointly drive the output. In the paper's min(i1, i2) example Rescale scores only the smaller input, while the RevealCancel rule shares the credit. Where inputs interact, the scores can hide a dependency that a more complete rule would show.

Propagation rules must support the network operations. Captum implements the Rescale rule and a limited set of nonlinearities; inaccessible operations in built-in recurrent modules can prevent attribution unless a supported implementation is used.

Two networks that compute exactly the same function can receive different DeepLIFT scores, because differences between a neuron and its reference do not obey the chain rule that gradients obey (Sundararajan et al., 2017, App. B). The scores therefore describe how the model is built as well as what it computes, which matters when comparing a model with a re-implemented or compressed version of it.

Feature contributions account for a particular output difference, not a causal effect in the world or a guaranteed change after deleting that feature. Correlated genomic bases or financial variables make that distinction important.

resources.title: Learning Important Features Through Propagating Activation Differences
resources.abstract: The purported "black box" nature of neural networks is a barrier to adoption in applications where interpretability is essential. Here we present DeepLIFT (Deep Learning Important FeaTures), a method for decomposing the output prediction of a neural network on a specific input by backpropagating the contributions of all neurons in the network to every feature of the input. DeepLIFT compares the activation of each neuron to its 'reference activation' and assigns contribution scores according to the difference. By optionally giving separate consideration to positive and negative contributions, DeepLIFT can also reveal dependencies which are missed by other approaches. Scores can be computed efficiently in a single backward pass. We apply DeepLIFT to models trained on MNIST and simulated genomic data, and show significant advantages over gradient-based methods. Video tutorial: http://goo.gl/qKb7pL, ICML slides: bit.ly/deeplifticmlslides, ICML talk: https://vimeo.com/238275076, code: http://goo.gl/RM8jvH.

resources.title: An Attribution Deep Learning Interpretation Model for Landslide Susceptibility Mapping in the Three Gorges Reservoir Area
resources.abstract: Deep learning (DL) models are increasingly used for landslide susceptibility mapping (LSM) due to their higher accuracy. However, due to the lack of explanations of the influence of input contributing factors by current DL models, accurately identifying the cause of each landslide remains challenging. This study proposes a novel interpretable DL model named Deep-Attention-LSF, which assigns significance scores to contributing factors at local levels for attributing landslide susceptibility. This model considers the significance scores of input factors to more accurately predict landslide occurrence. DeepLIFT is used as an attribution branching network for interpreting the relationship between input factors and each landslide event. Subsequently, a landslide classification network formed by combining convolutional neural network and long short-term memory is used to predict the landslide occurrence in the entire study area. The performance of Deep-Attention-LSF is tested using the landslide inventory map of Three Gorges reservoir area and the associated maps of 18 landslide-related factors. The accuracy, recall, precision, and F1-score of our model were 0.9645, 0.9583, 0.9676, and 0.9522, respectively. These suggest that our model outperformed the compared models, including self-attention LSM, frequency-ratio-attention LSM, bagging and random subspace naive bayes tree, gradient boosting decision tree, random forest, information value model and enhanced C5.0 decision tree model. Deep-Attention-LSF provided reasonable explanations for landslide attributions by comparison with field investigation reports for four specific landslide cases. Combining the interpretation of Deep-Attention-LSF with field investigations can provide more comprehensive information for evaluating specific landslides, providing a useful tool for landslide prevention and management.

techniques.name: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation
techniques.description: Layer-wise Relevance Propagation (LRP) explains a neural network's prediction by working backwards from the output to the inputs. It treats the prediction score as a quantity called relevance, then passes that relevance back through each layer in proportion to how much each neuron contributed in the forward pass. The rules for this redistribution are chosen to keep the total relevance roughly constant from layer to layer, so the input scores add up to the prediction apart from small amounts absorbed by bias terms and stabilisers. Different rules can be used for different types of layer. The result is a relevance score for each input, such as a pixel or a feature, with positive values for inputs that supported the prediction and negative values for inputs that counted against it.

example_use_cases.description: Identifying which pixels in chest X-rays contribute to pneumonia detection, helping radiologists verify AI diagnoses by highlighting anatomical regions the model considers relevant.

A perception team investigating a misclassified traffic-sign image draws the relevance map for the wrong class. The map shows the relevance sitting on a sticker and the background rather than on the sign itself, which tells the team to add training images with such clutter before the model is retested.

A bank's model-risk reviewers receive LRP relevance scores for a sample of declined applications scored by a neural network. They check that the inputs with the most relevance for the decline output are affordability measures and not proxy fields such as postcode, and file the scores with the decision record for audit.

limitations.description: Each layer type needs its own propagation rule, and a new layer type has none until someone derives one, so adapting LRP to a new architecture takes expertise and testing.
Rule selection (LRP-ε, LRP-γ and others) changes the resulting maps, so two analysts can produce different explanations of the same prediction, and choosing among them takes expertise.

Heatmaps are hard to validate. The original paper judges them by eye and with a pixel-flipping test, and notes that quality beyond visual assessment is an open question, so a plausible-looking map does not prove the model relies on the highlighted inputs.

Standard rules do not cover attention layers. Extensions for transformers, such as AttnLRP in the LXT library, exist but are recent and specific to certain architectures, so users of transformers or large language models must adopt them and confirm they match their model.

Bias handling and epsilon stabilisation can absorb or inject relevance, so input scores do not always sum exactly to the selected output. A report should document the accounting residual before claiming conservation.

resources.title: On Pixel-Wise Explanations for Non-Linear Classifier Decisions by Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation
resources.abstract: Understanding and interpreting classification decisions of automated image classification systems is of high value in many applications, as it allows to verify the reasoning of the system and provides additional information to the human expert. Although machine learning methods are solving very successfully a plethora of tasks, they have in most cases the disadvantage of acting as a black box, not providing any information about what made them arrive at a particular decision. This work proposes a general solution to the problem of understanding classification decisions by pixel-wise decomposition of nonlinear classifiers. We introduce a methodology that allows to visualize the contributions of single pixels to predictions for kernel-based classifiers over Bag of Words features and for multilayered neural networks. These pixel contributions can be visualized as heatmaps and are provided to a human expert who can intuitively not only verify the validity of the classification decision, but also focus further analysis on regions of potential interest. We evaluate our method for classifiers trained on PASCAL VOC 2009 images, synthetic image data containing geometric shapes, the MNIST handwritten digits data set and for the pre-trained ImageNet model available as part of the Caffe open source package.

resources.title: Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation: An Overview
Layer-Wise Relevance Propagation for Explaining Deep Neural Network Decisions in MRI-Based Alzheimer's Disease Classification
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks have led to state-of-the-art results in many medical imaging tasks including Alzheimer's disease (AD) detection based on structural magnetic resonance imaging (MRI) data. However, the network decisions are often perceived as being highly non-transparent, making it difficult to apply these algorithms in clinical routine. In this study, we propose using layer-wise relevance propagation (LRP) to visualize convolutional neural network decisions for AD based on MRI data. Similarly to other visualization methods, LRP produces a heatmap in the input space indicating the importance/relevance of each voxel contributing to the final classification outcome. In contrast to susceptibility maps produced by guided backpropagation ("Which change in voxels would change the outcome most?"), the LRP method is able to directly highlight positive contributions to the network classification in the input space. In particular, we show that (1) the LRP method is very specific for individuals ("Why does this person have AD?") with high inter-patient variability, (2) there is very little relevance for AD in healthy controls and (3) areas that exhibit a lot of relevance correlate well with what is known from literature. To quantify the latter, we compute size-corrected metrics of the summed relevance per brain area, e.g., relevance density or relevance gain. Although these metrics produce very individual "fingerprints" of relevance patterns for AD patients, a lot of importance is put on areas in the temporal lobe including the hippocampus. After discussing several limitations such as sensitivity toward the underlying model and computation parameters, we conclude that LRP might have a high potential to assist clinicians in explaining neural network decisions for diagnosing AD (and potentially other diseases) based on structural MRI data.

techniques.name: Contextual Decomposition
techniques.description: Contextual Decomposition explains why an LSTM, a neural network that reads text one word at a time, made a particular prediction. The user picks a word or phrase, and the method splits the network's output score into two parts: the part due to that phrase alone, and the part due to everything else, including how the phrase interacts with the words around it. Comparing a phrase's score with the scores of its parts reveals effects that word-by-word methods miss, such as a negation reversing the sentiment of the word that follows it. The split is tracked through the LSTM's internal gates, so the model itself is not changed or retrained. The output is a numerical score for each phrase examined.

example_use_cases.description: Analysing why an LSTM-based spam filter flagged an email by decomposing contributions from individual words ('free', 'urgent') versus their contextual interactions ('free trial' together).

A hospital analytics team checks an LSTM that flags clinical notes mentioning possible pneumonia. Contextual decomposition shows whether negated findings such as 'no evidence of pneumonia' push the score down, as intended, or whether the model reacts to the word 'pneumonia' alone, which tells the team if it needs retraining on negated examples before use.

A platform's trust-and-safety team handles an appeal against an LSTM toxicity classifier's removal of a post. The reviewing moderator is shown the phrases with the highest contextual decomposition scores, including whether a negation such as 'not stupid' was read correctly, so the moderator can judge whether the removal rested on the post's actual meaning.

limitations.description: Developed for LSTMs, whose gates the method uses to separate a phrase's own effect from its interactions. The source does not cover plain recurrent networks, transformers or attention models, so teams using those cannot apply the published method as it stands.
Needs internal states, gate parameters and classifier weights. Output labels or probabilities alone do not reveal the phrase-related and remaining-input components.

The user must choose each phrase to examine, and the published method handles contiguous phrases. The number of possible phrases grows quickly with text length, so scanning a whole document for interactions is costly and easy to leave incomplete.

The split relies on linearising the gate and activation functions and averaging over orderings of the terms. Interaction scores are therefore approximate, and the source validates them only on sentiment tasks (Stanford Sentiment Treebank, Yelp), so scores on other tasks need checking independently.

Components combine additively in hidden states and class scores before the probability transformation. They should not be read as independent probabilities or as the exact effect of deleting a phrase.

resources.title: Beyond Word Importance: Contextual Decomposition to Extract Interactions from LSTMs
resources.abstract: The driving force behind the recent success of LSTMs has been their ability to learn complex and non-linear relationships. Consequently, our inability to describe these relationships has led to LSTMs being characterized as black boxes. To this end, we introduce contextual decomposition (CD), an interpretation algorithm for analysing individual predictions made by standard LSTMs, without any changes to the underlying model. By decomposing the output of a LSTM, CD captures the contributions of combinations of words or variables to the final prediction of an LSTM. On the task of sentiment analysis with the Yelp and SST data sets, we show that CD is able to reliably identify words and phrases of contrasting sentiment, and how they are combined to yield the LSTM's final prediction. Using the phrase-level labels in SST, we also demonstrate that CD is able to successfully extract positive and negative negations from an LSTM, something which has not previously been done.

resources.title: Interpreting patient-Specific risk prediction using contextual decomposition of BiLSTMs: Application to children with asthma
resources.abstract: Background Predictive modeling with longitudinal electronic health record (EHR) data offers great promise for accelerating personalized medicine and better informs clinical decision-making. Recently, deep learning models have achieved state-of-the-art performance for many healthcare prediction tasks. However, deep models lack interpretability, which is integral to successful decision-making and can lead to better patient care. In this paper, we build upon the contextual decomposition (CD) method, an algorithm for producing importance scores from long short-term memory networks (LSTMs). We extend the method to bidirectional LSTMs (BiLSTMs) and use it in the context of predicting future clinical outcomes using patients’ EHR historical visits. Methods We use a real EHR dataset comprising 11071 patients, to evaluate and compare CD interpretations from LSTM and BiLSTM models. First, we train LSTM and BiLSTM models for the task of predicting which pre-school children with respiratory system-related complications will have asthma at school-age. After that, we conduct quantitative and qualitative analysis to evaluate the CD interpretations produced by the contextual decomposition of the trained models. In addition, we develop an interactive visualization to demonstrate the utility of CD scores in explaining predicted outcomes. Results Our experimental evaluation demonstrate that whenever a clear visit-level pattern exists, the models learn that pattern and the contextual decomposition can appropriately attribute the prediction to the correct pattern. In addition, the results confirm that the CD scores agree to a large extent with the importance scores generated using logistic regression coefficients. Our main insight was that rather than interpreting the attribution of individual visits to the predicted outcome, we could instead attribute a model’s prediction to a group of visits. Conclusion We presented a quantitative and qualitative evidence that CD interpretations can explain patient-specific predictions using CD attributions of individual visits or a group of visits.

techniques.name: Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations
techniques.description: LIME (Local Interpretable Model-agnostic Explanations) explains individual predictions by approximating the complex model's behaviour in a small neighbourhood around a specific instance. It works by creating perturbed versions of the input (e.g., removing words from text, changing pixel values in images, or varying feature values), obtaining the model's predictions for these variations, and training a simple interpretable model (typically linear regression) weighted by proximity to the original instance. The coefficients of this local surrogate model reveal which features most influenced the specific prediction.

example_use_cases.description: Explaining why a specific patient received a high-risk diagnosis by showing which symptoms (fever, blood pressure, age) contributed most to the prediction, helping doctors validate the AI's reasoning.
Debugging a text classifier's misclassification of a movie review by highlighting which words (e.g., sarcastic phrases) confused the model, enabling targeted model improvements.

Showing insurance customers the claim features that most influenced an automated approval or denial. A reviewer first checks that the explanation is stable across repeated runs and plausible for that claim, because it approximates the model locally and may not match its full reasoning.

limitations.description: Explanations can be unstable due to random sampling, producing different results across multiple runs.
The linear surrogate may poorly approximate highly non-linear model behaviour in the local region.
Defining the neighbourhood size and perturbation strategy requires careful tuning for each data type.
Can be computationally expensive for explaining many instances due to repeated model queries.

Assumes features are independent when generating perturbations, producing unrealistic out-of-distribution samples for datasets with correlated features. This can generate misleading attribution scores when inputs share strong correlations (e.g., age and income in credit scoring, comorbidities in clinical data).

resources.title: "Why Should I Trust You?": Explaining the Predictions of Any Classifier
resources.abstract: Despite widespread adoption, machine learning models remain mostly black boxes. Understanding the reasons behind predictions is, however, quite important in assessing trust, which is fundamental if one plans to take action based on a prediction, or when choosing whether to deploy a new model. Such understanding also provides insights into the model, which can be used to transform an untrustworthy model or prediction into a trustworthy one. In this work, we propose LIME, a novel explanation technique that explains the predictions of any classifier in an interpretable and faithful manner, by learning an interpretable model locally around the prediction. We also propose a method to explain models by presenting representative individual predictions and their explanations in a non-redundant way, framing the task as a submodular optimization problem. We demonstrate the flexibility of these methods by explaining different models for text (e.g. random forests) and image classification (e.g. neural networks). We show the utility of explanations via novel experiments, both simulated and with human subjects, on various scenarios that require trust: deciding if one should trust a prediction, choosing between models, improving an untrustworthy classifier, and identifying why a classifier should not be trusted.

Evaluating Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanations on Clinical Machine Learning Classification Models
resources.abstract: The usage of black-box classification models within the healthcare field is highly dependent on being interpretable by the receiver. Local Interpretable Model-Agnostic Explanation (LIME) provides a patient-specific explanation for a given classification, thus enhancing the possibility for any complex classifier to serve as a safety aid within a clinical setting. However, research on if the explanation provided by LIME is relevant to clinicians is limited and there is no current framework for how an evaluation of LIME is to be performed. To evaluate the clinical relevance of the explanations provided by LIME, this study has investigated how physician's independent explanations for classified observations compare with explanations provided by LIME. Additionally, the clinical relevance and the experienced reliance on the explanations provided by LIME have been evaluated by field experts. The results indicate that the explanation provided by LIME is clinically relevant and has a very high concordance with the explanations provided by physicians. Furthermore, trust and reliance on LIME are fairly high amongst clinicians. The study proposes a framework for further research within the area.

techniques.name: Ridge Regression Surrogates
techniques.description: A ridge regression surrogate approximates a complex model with a linear equation fitted to the complex model's own predictions. The complex model is run on a set of inputs, and ridge regression, a linear model with a penalty that keeps coefficients stable when features are correlated, is fitted to reproduce its outputs. Each coefficient then shows roughly how far a feature moves the complex model's output, averaged over those inputs. Fidelity, often reported as R-squared (the share of the model's variation the surrogate reproduces on held-out inputs), shows how far the coefficients can be trusted. They describe the complex model, not the real world.

example_use_cases.description: A model-risk team at a bank fits a ridge surrogate to a gradient-boosted credit-scoring model's scores on a held-out sample, reports how closely the surrogate reproduces them, and uses the standardised coefficients to brief the model-risk committee on which inputs drive scores overall.

A hospital analytics team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural network that predicts readmission risk from tabular records, to check that the features driving the network's predictions overall, such as age and prior admissions, are plausible to clinicians. The findings concern the network, not what causes readmission.

An energy company's forecasting team fits a ridge surrogate to a neural-network load forecaster using a year of hourly weather and calendar inputs, and reads the standardised coefficients to confirm that temperature and time of day dominate. A low R-squared during heatwaves leads the team to record that the surrogate does not describe the model in that regime.

An insurer's compliance team gives a regulator a ridge surrogate of its pricing model together with held-out R-squared and a table of each feature's contribution to a sample of quotes, so the regulator can check the stated drivers against the model's actual outputs.

limitations.description: A linear surrogate cannot represent interactions or thresholds. Where the complex model relies on them, the surrogate fits its predictions poorly and its coefficients describe a different model. Report held-out R-squared and treat a low value as a failed surrogate.

A good average fit can hide poor fit in parts of the input space, such as rare groups or extreme values, so the coefficients may be wrong for exactly the cases that matter. Check fidelity within subgroups and near decision boundaries.
There is no agreed fidelity level above which a surrogate can be trusted. Whether 50%, 80% or 99% of variance explained is enough depends on the use, so the reviewer has to set and justify a cut-off.

Ridge shrinks every coefficient and shares weight between correlated features. Coefficient sizes depend on the penalty strength and on feature scaling, so compare them only after standardising the features, and report the penalty used.

The surrogate explains the complex model's behaviour on the sampled inputs, not the real-world link between features and outcomes. Reading its coefficients as causes, or as evidence about the data, will mislead.

techniques.name: Contrastive Explanation Method
techniques.description: The Contrastive Explanation Method (CEM) explains one prediction of a classifier, such as a neural network, by describing what is present and what is absent in the input. A pertinent positive is the smallest set of features already present that is enough for the model to give the same prediction. A pertinent negative is the smallest set of features not currently present that would change the prediction to a different class if they were added. CEM finds both by solving an optimisation problem that searches for the smallest change to the input, and it can use an autoencoder (a model trained to reconstruct realistic inputs) to keep the changed inputs realistic. An explanation reads like 'this digit is a 3 because these strokes are present and because a short bar at the top is absent', since adding that bar would make it a 5.

example_use_cases.description: A procurement team uses a neural-network model that rates invoices as low, medium or high risk. For a high-risk invoice, the pertinent positives are the few triggered events that are enough for that rating, such as a large amount and a vendor with only a PO box. The pertinent negatives are events that did not occur but would lower the rating if they had, such as the vendor being registered. Reviewers check both before blocking payment.

A clinician reviews a decision-support model that suggests flu rather than pneumonia for a patient. The pertinent positives are the findings that are enough for that suggestion, such as cough, cold and fever. The pertinent negatives are findings that are absent but would move the suggestion to pneumonia if present, such as sputum and chills. The clinician compares both with their own reasoning to judge whether the model weighs the right findings.

A council uses a model to screen applications for housing support. When an application is declined, the pertinent negatives show which missing items, such as proof of tenancy, would have changed the outcome if present. A caseworker checks that each item is something the applicant can provide, then includes it in the decision notice.

limitations.description: Each explanation needs its own optimisation run for a single instance, so explaining many decisions is slow. Models whose gradients cannot be accessed need numerical gradient estimates, which slows it further.

Several settings shape the result, including how strongly the search favours small changes, how confident the model must be in the new class, and whether an autoencoder is used. Different settings can give different pertinent positives and negatives for the same instance, so they need checking with someone who knows the domain.

Changed inputs can be unrealistic. Without an autoencoder trained on good-quality data, a pertinent negative may describe an input that could never occur, so the explanation says little about real cases. Where data is scarce or poor, a good autoencoder may not be possible.

Absence has to be defined by the user. CEM adds or removes features relative to a value that stands for no signal, such as a blank pixel, and a poor choice gives meaningless pertinent negatives. This is natural for images and binary indicators, and needs domain judgement for continuous or categorical tabular data.

A pertinent negative is the smallest change the model responds to, not advice a person can act on. It may involve a feature that cannot be changed, such as age, and nothing in the method checks that the change is feasible. It is most useful when the two classes are close; if they are very different, there can be too many pertinent negatives to read.

resources.title: Explanations based on the Missing: Towards Contrastive Explanations with Pertinent Negatives
resources.abstract: In this paper we propose a novel method that provides contrastive explanations justifying the classification of an input by a black box classifier such as a deep neural network. Given an input we find what should be %necessarily and minimally and sufficiently present (viz. important object pixels in an image) to justify its classification and analogously what should be minimally and necessarily \emph{absent} (viz. certain background pixels). We argue that such explanations are natural for humans and are used commonly in domains such as health care and criminology. What is minimally but critically \emph{absent} is an important part of an explanation, which to the best of our knowledge, has not been explicitly identified by current explanation methods that explain predictions of neural networks. We validate our approach on three real datasets obtained from diverse domains; namely, a handwritten digits dataset MNIST, a large procurement fraud dataset and a brain activity strength dataset. In all three cases, we witness the power of our approach in generating precise explanations that are also easy for human experts to understand and evaluate.

Understanding How CNNs Recognize Facial Expressions: A Case Study with LIME and CEM
resources.abstract: Recognizing facial expressions has been a persistent goal in the scientific community. Since the rise of artificial intelligence, convolutional neural networks (CNN) have become popular to recognize facial expressions, as images can be directly used as input. Current CNN models can achieve high recognition rates, but they give no clue about their reasoning process. Explainable artificial intelligence (XAI) has been developed as a means to help to interpret the results obtained by machine learning models. When dealing with images, one of the most-used XAI techniques is LIME. LIME highlights the areas of the image that contribute to a classification. As an alternative to LIME, the CEM method appeared, providing explanations in a way that is natural for human classification: besides highlighting what is sufficient to justify a classification, it also identifies what should be absent to maintain it and to distinguish it from another classification. This study presents the results of comparing LIME and CEM applied over complex images such as facial expression images. While CEM could be used to explain the results on images described with a reduced number of features, LIME would be the method of choice when dealing with images described with a huge number of features.

techniques.name: ANCHOR
techniques.description: ANCHOR explains one prediction of a black-box classifier with an if-then rule, called an anchor, such as 'age > 30 AND income < £50k'. An anchor names a small set of feature conditions under which the model keeps giving the same prediction, whatever the other features are. To find one, the method fixes the conditions, varies the other features by sampling, asks the model for a prediction each time, and searches for the broadest rule that holds in at least a chosen share of the samples, commonly 95%. Each anchor comes with its estimated precision and its coverage, the share of cases to which it applies. Both figures describe the model's behaviour on the sampled variations, not on real cases, and continuous features are first grouped into ranges.

example_use_cases.description: A model-validation team at a lender computes anchors for a sample of declined applications from a gradient-boosted credit model. It checks that the conditions holding each decision, such as a low credit-score band together with recent missed payments, match credit policy, and reads each rule's coverage to see how many other applications it applies to.

A hospital data team explains individual alerts from a tabular sepsis-risk model with anchors, and a clinician checks whether the conditions in each rule, such as raised temperature and white-cell count, are clinically sensible or point to an artefact such as the ward an admission came from.

An employer's compliance team gives a reviewer the anchor behind a shortlisting prediction, with its precision and coverage. The reviewer tests the rule on other applications and can challenge it if it leans on an attribute that should not matter, such as age.

limitations.description: The stated precision is measured on perturbed samples from a chosen sampling distribution, not on real cases. If that distribution produces unrealistic inputs, or is skewed by an unbalanced training set, the figure can overstate how far the rule can be relied on.

An anchor covers only the inputs its conditions match, often a small share. In the original experiments average coverage ranged from about 1% to 29% on tabular data, so one anchor says little about the model as a whole. Choosing a set of anchors helps but adds effort.

Predictions close to the model's decision boundary, or of rare classes, need long, very specific rules with little coverage, which add little insight. Strict precision thresholds make this more likely.

Continuous features must be grouped into ranges before rules can be stated, and the grouping changes which anchors are found. Too coarse hides boundaries, and too fine gives narrow rules with little coverage.

Each anchor needs many queries to the model, so run time depends on how fast the model is and on the number of features. The method is built for classifiers, so a numeric output must first be turned into classes.

resources.title: Anchors: High-Precision Model-Agnostic Explanations
resources.abstract: We introduce a novel model-agnostic system that explains the behavior of complex models with high-precision rules called anchors, representing local, "sufficient" conditions for predictions. We propose an algorithm to efficiently compute these explanations for any black-box model with high-probability guarantees. We demonstrate the flexibility of anchors by explaining a myriad of different models for different domains and tasks. In a user study, we show that anchors enable users to predict how a model would behave on unseen instances with less effort and higher precision, as compared to existing linear explanations or no explanations.

Interpretability in HealthCare A Comparative Study of Local Machine Learning Interpretability Techniques
resources.abstract: Although complex machine learning models (e.g., Random Forest, Neural Networks) are commonly outperforming the traditional simple interpretable models (e.g., Linear Regression, Decision Tree), in the healthcare domain, clinicians find it hard to understand and trust these complex models due to the lack of intuition and explanation of their predictions. With the new General Data Protection Regulation (GDPR), the importance for plausibility and verifiability of the predictions made by machine learning models has become essential. To tackle this challenge, recently, several machine learning interpretability techniques have been developed and introduced. In general, the main aim of these interpretability techniques is to shed light and provide insights into the predictions process of the machine learning models and explain how the model predictions have resulted. However, in practice, assessing the quality of the explanations provided by the various interpretability techniques is still questionable. In this paper, we present a comprehensive experimental evaluation of three recent and popular local model agnostic interpretability techniques, namely, LIME, SHAP and Anchors on different types of real-world healthcare data. Our experimental evaluation covers different aspects for its comparison including identity, stability, separability, similarity, execution time and bias detection. The results of our experiments show that LIME achieves the lowest performance for the identity metric and the highest performance for the separability metric across all datasets included in this study. On average, SHAP has the smallest average time to output explanation across all datasets included in this study. For detecting the bias, SHAP enables the participants to better detect the bias.

Each shortlisting decision from the screening model can be given to a reviewer as a rule with its precision and coverage, so that the reviewer can test the rule on other applications.
Every reason given for an individual model output states its own coverage, so a reviewer knows which other cases the reason applies to and which it does not.

techniques.name: RuleFit
techniques.description: RuleFit builds a predictive model that a person can read: a short list of if-then rules plus a few ordinary feature weights. It first trains an ensemble of decision trees (many small trees whose outputs are combined) and turns each branch into a candidate rule, such as 'IF age > 50 AND income < £30k'. It then fits a linear model over those rules and the original features using the lasso, a penalty that sets many weights to exactly zero, so only the most useful terms remain. The surviving rules and weights can be read directly, and each term has an importance score, overall and for single predictions. Fitted to real outcomes, the result can replace an opaque model; fitted to an opaque model's predictions, it is a surrogate that approximates that model, and its fit should then be checked.

example_use_cases.description: A telecoms analytics team fits RuleFit to the predictions of its gradient-boosted churn model rather than to the churn labels, to get a short list of rules that approximates the model. Marketing staff read the top rules, and the team reports how closely the rules reproduce the model's predictions before anyone relies on them.

A lender replaces an opaque default-risk model with a RuleFit model fitted to repayment outcomes. For one declined application, the importance scores show which few rules and income or debt terms drove its score, and the validation team checks them against credit policy.

A hospital team builds an admission-risk model as a RuleFit model fitted directly to patient outcomes, so that clinicians and the ethics committee can read the whole model, a few rules such as 'IF systolic_bp > 140 AND diabetes = true' plus a handful of weights. The team counts the active rules first and keeps the model only if it is short enough to read.

limitations.description: The lasso can leave many rules active, and a model with hundreds of active terms is no longer readable. Rules also approximate smooth linear trends poorly and need many pieces to do so. Count the non-zero terms before calling the model interpretable.

Rules overlap and are often correlated, so a rule's weight cannot be read on its own. 'Temperature above 15' is also true wherever 'temperature above 10' is. With correlated inputs, rules can also suggest interactions that are not in the real relationship.

Tree size sets how long rules can be and which interactions can appear. Shallow trees give short, readable rules but miss high-order interactions, and deep trees capture them at the cost of long rules. No single depth suits every problem.

Fitted to a black-box model's predictions, RuleFit only approximates that model. Without a fidelity check, such as agreement on held-out inputs, its rules describe the surrogate and may not describe the model they are meant to explain.

resources.title: Predictive learning via rule ensembles
resources.abstract: General regression and classification models are constructed as linear combinations of simple rules derived from the data. Each rule consists of a conjunction of a small number of simple statements concerning the values of individual input variables. These rule ensembles are shown to produce predictive accuracy comparable to the best methods. However, their principal advantage lies in interpretation. Because of its simple form, each rule is easy to understand, as is its influence on individual predictions, selected subsets of predictions, or globally over the entire space of joint input variable values. Similarly, the degree of relevance of the respective input variables can be assessed globally, locally in different regions of the input space, or at individual prediction points. Techniques are presented for automatically identifying those variables that are involved in interactions with other variables, the strength and degree of those interactions, as well as the identities of the other variables with which they interact. Graphical representations are used to visualize both main and interaction effects.

RuleFit-Based Nomogram Using Inflammatory Indicators for Predicting Survival in Nasopharyngeal Carcinoma, a Bi-Center Study
resources.abstract: Purpose: Traditional prognostic studies utilized different cut-off values, without evaluating potential information contained in inflammation-related hematological indicators. Using the interpretable machine-learning algorithm RuleFit, this study aimed to explore valuable inflammatory rules reflecting prognosis in nasopharyngeal carcinoma (NPC) patients. Patients and Methods: In total, 1706 biopsy-proven NPC patients treated in two independent hospitals (1320 and 386) between January 2010 and March 2014 were included. RuleFit was used to develop risk-predictive rules using hematological indicators with no distributive difference between the two centers. Time-event-dependent hematological rules were further selected by stepwise multivariate Cox analysis. Combining high-efficiency hematological rules and clinical predictors, a final model was established. Models based on other algorithms (AutoML, Lasso) and clinical predictors were built for comparison, as well as a reported nomogram. Area under the receiver operating characteristic curve (AUROC) and concordance index (C-index) were used to verify the predictive precision of different models. A site-based app was established for convenience. Results: RuleFit identified 22 combined baseline hematological rules, achieving AUROCs of 0.69 and 0.64 in the training and validation cohorts, respectively. By contrast, the AUROCs of the optimal contrast model based on AutoML were 1.00 and 0.58. For overall survival, the final model had a much higher C-index than the base model using TN staging in two cohorts (0.769 vs 0.717, P < 0.001; 0.752 vs 0.688, P < 0.001), and showing great generalizability in training and validation cohorts. The two models based on RuleFit rules performed best, compared with other models. As for other endpoints, the final model showed a similar trend. Kaplan–Meier curve exhibited 22.9% (390/1706) patients were “misclassified” by AJCC staging, but the final model could assess risk classification accurately. Conclusion: The proposed final models based on inflammation-related rules based on RuleFit showed significantly elevated predictive performance.

techniques.name: Differential Privacy
techniques.description: Differential privacy puts a mathematical limit on what a published result reveals about any one person. The data holder adds random noise, drawn for example from a Laplace or Gaussian distribution, to each answer before release, such as a count, an average or a table of statistics, so the answer would look almost the same with or without any one person's data. The amount of noise depends on how much one person could change the answer (its sensitivity) and on a privacy budget called epsilon, which sets how far the two cases may differ (the Gaussian mechanism adds a second, small parameter, delta, for the chance of exceeding that limit). A smaller epsilon means more noise, a stronger guarantee and less accurate answers, and each release spends part of the budget. The guarantee covers whether a person's data took part, not conclusions about the wider population that the results legitimately show.

example_use_cases.description: A national statistics office adds calibrated noise to published census tables so that no single household's presence changes the results by more than a set amount. Statisticians use the epsilon setting to decide how much accuracy small areas must give up.

A health authority publishes weekly hospital admission counts by postcode district with Laplace noise added, so a rare diagnosis in a small district cannot be tied to one patient. Its privacy officer sets a yearly budget and decides how many weekly releases it can cover.

An analytics team lets internal analysts query customer purchase data only through an interface that adds noise and tracks each analyst's privacy budget. The data protection lead uses the budget log to decide when an analyst must stop querying.

A model-evaluation team publishes noisy aggregate performance counts for declared groups. It documents the protected unit, sensitivity bound, noise mechanism and cumulative privacy budget so reviewers can interpret the release's guarantee.

limitations.description: Noise lowers accuracy, and for a given epsilon the noise on a count does not shrink as the dataset grows, so small groups, rare categories and fine-grained tables suffer most. A strong guarantee (small epsilon) can make statistics for small subgroups unusable.
Setting the privacy budget (epsilon) requires expertise and careful consideration of the privacy-utility trade-off, with no universal guidelines for appropriate values across different applications.

Each release spends part of a fixed privacy budget, and the epsilons add up across releases. Once the budget is spent, no further analysis of the same data is possible without weakening the guarantee, so releases must be planned in advance.

The guarantee depends on correct sensitivity analysis: if a query's sensitivity is underestimated, or one person can contribute many records, too little noise is added and the stated epsilon no longer holds.

The guarantee concerns whether one person's data took part, not what the results show about the population. Conclusions that hold for everyone still apply to each individual, and protection weakens for groups, such as a family, by a factor equal to the group size.

resources.title: The Algorithmic Foundations of Differential Privacy
resources.abstract: The problem of privacy-preserving data analysis has a long history spanning multiple disciplines. As electronic data about individuals becomes increasingly detailed, and as technology enables ever more powerful collection and curation of these data, the need increases for a robust, meaningful, and mathematically rigorous definition of privacy, together with a computationally rich class of algorithms that satisfy this definition. Differential Privacy is such a definition. After motivating and discussing the meaning of differential privacy, the preponderance of this monograph is devoted to fundamental techniques for achieving differential privacy, and application of these techniques in creative combinations, using the query-release problem as an ongoing example. A key point is that, by rethinking the computational goal, one can often obtain far better results than would be achieved by methodically replacing each step of a non-private computation with a differentially private implementation. Despite some astonishingly powerful computational results, there are still fundamental limitations — not just on what can be achieved with differential privacy but on what can be achieved with any method that protects against a complete breakdown in privacy. Virtually all the algorithms discussed herein maintain differential privacy against adversaries of arbitrary computational power. Certain algorithms are computationally intensive, others are efficient. Computational complexity for the adversary and the algorithm are both discussed. We then turn from fundamentals to applications other than queryrelease, discussing differentially private methods for mechanism design and machine learning. The vast majority of the literature on differentially private algorithms considers a single, static, database that is subject to many analyses. Differential privacy in other models, including distributed databases and computations on data streams is discussed. Finally, we note that this work is meant as a thorough introduction to the problems and techniques of differential privacy, but is not intended to be an exhaustive survey — there is by now a vast amount of work in differential privacy, and we can cover only a small portion of it.

resources.abstract: The Census TopDown Algorithm (TDA) is a disclosure avoidance system using differential privacy for privacy-loss accounting.The algorithm ingests the final, edited version of the 2020 Census data and the final tabulation geographic definitions.The algorithm then creates noisy versions of key queries on the data, referred to as measurements, using zero-Concentrated Differential Privacy.Another key aspect of the TDA are invariants, statistics that the Census Bureau has determined, as matter of policy, to exclude from the privacyloss accounting.The TDA postprocesses the measurements together with the invariants to produce a Microdata Detail File (MDF) that contains one record for each person and one record for each housing unit enumerated in the 2020 Census.The MDF is passed to the 2020 Census tabulation system to produce the 2020 Census Redistricting Data (P.L. 94-171) Summary File.This article describes the mathematics and testing of the TDA for this purpose.

resources.title: RAPPOR
resources.abstract: Randomized Aggregatable Privacy-Preserving Ordinal Response, or RAPPOR, is a technology for crowdsourcing statistics from end-user client software, anonymously, with strong privacy guarantees. In short, RAPPORs allow the forest of client data to be studied, without permitting the possibility of looking at individual trees. By applying randomized response in a novel manner, RAPPOR provides the mechanisms for such collection as well as for efficient, high-utility analysis of the collected data. In particular, RAPPOR permits statistics to be collected on the population of client-side strings with strong privacy guarantees for each client, and without linkability of their reports. This paper describes and motivates RAPPOR, details its differential-privacy and utility guarantees, discusses its practical deployment and properties in the face of different attack models, and, finally, gives results of its application to both synthetic and real-world data.

techniques.name: Conformal Prediction
techniques.description: Conformal prediction wraps any trained model so that, instead of a single answer, it returns a set of plausible answers (an interval, for a numeric prediction) that contains the true outcome at a chosen rate, such as at least 95% of the time. It first scores, on a calibration set of labelled data kept apart from training, how unusual each known outcome looks given the model's prediction, using a nonconformity score, and for a new case it keeps every candidate answer whose score falls below a threshold taken from those calibration scores. A diagnostic model might then return 'cancer or benign tumour' rather than 'likely cancer', and with a suitable score the sets grow larger where the model is less certain. The guarantee is distribution-free, meaning it assumes nothing about the shape of the data, but it does assume the calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. It holds on average over all cases, not within each subgroup, unless the calibration is done separately within each predefined group (Mondrian conformal prediction), which needs enough calibration cases in every group.

example_use_cases.description: A medicinal chemistry team screening compounds in silico builds prediction sets of the protein targets each compound may be active against, at 95% coverage. Compounds with a single-target set go to lab testing for that target, and those with several targets go to a wider panel, so costly experiments follow how uncertain the model is.

Providing transparent multi-class predictions in judicial risk assessment by showing all plausible risk categories at the stated coverage level, enabling judges to see the full range of possibilities rather than just a single point estimate.

A university predicts whether first-year students will complete their degree and offers early support when the 90% prediction set includes 'withdraws'. To keep that 90% true for every group, not only on average, the data team calibrates the sets separately within each demographic group, then checks coverage and average set size per group on held-out students. A group with too few calibration cases is reported as not covered by the guarantee.

limitations.description: Sets can be wide enough to be useless. A multi-class set holding most classes, or an interval spanning the plausible range, meets the coverage target but tells the decision-maker little, and sets containing opposing outcomes make decisions hard. Width depends on the model's quality and the scoring rule chosen, and the guarantee says nothing about it.

Needs labelled calibration data kept apart from training. On small datasets that means less data to train on, or a coarse and unstable coverage level, and variants that avoid a separate calibration set need several model fits.

The guarantee assumes calibration data and new cases are exchangeable, roughly that they come from the same source in no particular order. Drift, a changed population or strongly time-ordered data break it, and coverage then falls below target with no warning. In Shafer and Vovk's example, a nominal 5% error rate rose to 8% on a systematically different test set.

Coverage is guaranteed on average over all cases, not for each individual or subgroup, so a model can reach 95% overall while covering a minority group far less often. Mondrian calibration fixes this only for predefined, non-overlapping groups. It needs each new case's group at prediction time and is unstable when a group has few calibration cases (MAPIE's tutorial gives under 200 as an example).

Cost depends on the variant. Split conformal prediction adds little beyond scoring a held-out set, but full conformal prediction re-evaluates every candidate outcome and cross-conformal variants refit the model several times, which can be prohibitive for large models or real-time use.

resources.title: A tutorial on conformal prediction
resources.abstract: Conformal prediction uses past experience to determine precise levels of confidence in new predictions. Given an error probability $ε$, together with a method that makes a prediction $\hat{y}$ of a label $y$, it produces a set of labels, typically containing $\hat{y}$, that also contains $y$ with probability $1-ε$. Conformal prediction can be applied to any method for producing $\hat{y}$: a nearest-neighbor method, a support-vector machine, ridge regression, etc.   Conformal prediction is designed for an on-line setting in which labels are predicted successively, each one being revealed before the next is predicted. The most novel and valuable feature of conformal prediction is that if the successive examples are sampled independently from the same distribution, then the successive predictions will be right $1-ε$ of the time, even though they are based on an accumulating dataset rather than on independent datasets.   In addition to the model under which successive examples are sampled independently, other on-line compression models can also use conformal prediction. The widely used Gaussian linear model is one of these.   This tutorial presents a self-contained account of the theory of conformal prediction and works through several numerical examples. A more comprehensive treatment of the topic is provided in "Algorithmic Learning in a Random World", by Vladimir Vovk, Alex Gammerman, and Glenn Shafer (Springer, 2005).

resources.title: Estimating diagnostic uncertainty in artificial intelligence assisted pathology using conformal prediction
resources.abstract: Unreliable predictions can occur when an artificial intelligence (AI) system is presented with data it has not been exposed to during training. We demonstrate the use of conformal prediction to detect unreliable predictions, using histopathological diagnosis and grading of prostate biopsies as example. We digitized 7788 prostate biopsies from 1192 men in the STHLM3 diagnostic study, used for training, and 3059 biopsies from 676 men used for testing. With conformal prediction, 1 in 794 (0.1%) predictions is incorrect for cancer diagnosis (compared to 14 errors [2%] without conformal prediction) while 175 (22%) of the predictions are flagged as unreliable when the AI-system is presented with new data from the same lab and scanner that it was trained on. Conformal prediction could with small samples ( N = 49 for external scanner, N = 10 for external lab and scanner, and N = 12 for external lab, scanner and pathology assessment) detect systematic differences in external data leading to worse predictive performance. The AI-system with conformal prediction commits 3 (2%) errors for cancer detection in cases of atypical prostate tissue compared to 44 (25%) without conformal prediction, while the system flags 143 (80%) unreliable predictions. We conclude that conformal prediction can increase patient safety of AI-systems.

Prediction-set coverage on the latest quarter of live data stays within the agreed margin of its nominal level, so there is no sign that the exchangeability assumption has broken down in deployment.

techniques.name: Platt Scaling
techniques.description: Platt scaling turns a classifier's raw scores into calibrated probabilities, meaning that among the cases given a probability of 0.3, about 30 per cent turn out to be positive. It was introduced for support vector machines, whose outputs are distances from a decision boundary rather than probabilities, and applies to any binary classifier that produces a real-valued score. After the classifier is trained, a two-parameter logistic (sigmoid) curve, P(y = 1 | f) = 1 / (1 + exp(A·f + B)), is fitted by maximum likelihood to map each score f to a probability, using labelled cases the classifier was not trained on, taken from a held-out set or from cross-validation folds. The fitted curve is strictly monotonic, so the order of cases and ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve (how well the scores separate the two classes) are unchanged; only the probability attached to each case moves. The output is a recalibrated model, assessed before and after with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and with the Brier score or log loss (two measures of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened).

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's credit-risk team finds that its gradient-boosted default model ranks applicants well but squeezes predicted default probabilities towards the middle of the range. Before the probabilities feed expected-loss provisioning, the team fits Platt scaling on a held-out year of loan outcomes and checks on a reliability diagram that predicted and observed default rates agree in every score decile.

A benefits agency uses a linear support vector machine to flag claims for manual review, but its margin scores mean nothing to caseworkers. The team applies Platt scaling so the review screen can show the probability that a claim needs correcting, publishes the calibration curve in the caseworker guidance, and explains that the figure is a rate across similar claims rather than a verdict on the individual.

limitations.description: The sigmoid shape is an assumption. It corrects the S-shaped distortion typical of support vector machines and boosted trees, whose probabilities bunch towards the middle, but not the reverse distortion of overconfident models such as naive Bayes, whose probabilities pile up near 0 and 1. Where the reliability diagram shows that pattern, a flexible method such as isotonic regression is needed.

It works best when the classifier's scores for the two classes are spread in a similar way (roughly normal with equal variance). In highly imbalanced problems the scores of the two classes do not have equal spread, so the sigmoid can be a poor match for the data.

The curve should be fitted on labelled cases that played no part in training. The classifier separates its own training data better than new data, so a curve fitted to training scores overstates confidence in use; the cost is a held-out calibration set taken from scarce labelled data, or cross-validation with several model fits.

A single curve fitted across the whole population does not make the model calibrated within each subgroup. In a deployed malnutrition-risk model, recalibration improved calibration within each race and sex group, yet intercepts and slopes still differed significantly between Black and White patients. Fitting a curve per group needs group membership at prediction time, which may be unavailable or unlawful to use, and enough labelled cases in every group.

Recalibration changes every probability, so a decision threshold chosen on the raw scores no longer flags the same cases. After logistic recalibration of a deployed malnutrition-risk model, specificity rose from 0.74 to 0.93 and sensitivity fell from 0.75 to 0.35, so the cut-off has to be reset against the cost of each kind of error and the downstream process checked again.

resources.title: Assessing calibration and bias of a deployed machine learning malnutrition prediction model within a large healthcare system
resources.abstract: Malnutrition is a frequently underdiagnosed condition leading to increased morbidity, mortality, and healthcare costs. The Mount Sinai Health System (MSHS) deployed a machine learning model (MUST-Plus) to detect malnutrition upon hospital admission. However, in diverse patient groups, a poorly calibrated model may lead to misdiagnosis, exacerbating health care disparities. We explored the model’s calibration across different variables and methods to improve calibration. Data from adult patients admitted to five MSHS hospitals from January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, were analyzed. We compared MUST-Plus prediction to the registered dietitian’s formal assessment. Hierarchical calibration was assessed and compared between the recalibration sample (N = 49,562) of patients admitted between January 1, 2021 - December 31, 2022, and the hold-out sample (N = 17,278) of patients admitted between January 1, 2023 - September 30, 2023. Statistical differences in calibration metrics were tested using bootstrapping with replacement. Before recalibration, the overall model calibration intercept was −1.17 (95% CI: −1.20, −1.14), slope was 1.37 (95% CI: 1.34, 1.40), and Brier score was 0.26 (95% CI: 0.25, 0.26). Both weak and moderate measures of calibration were significantly different between White and Black patients and between male and female patients. Logistic recalibration significantly improved calibration of the model across race and gender in the hold-out sample. The original MUST-Plus model showed significant differences in calibration between White vs. Black patients. It also overestimated malnutrition in females compared to males. Logistic recalibration effectively reduced miscalibration across all patient subgroups. Continual monitoring and timely recalibration can improve model accuracy.

Each flagged claim is shown to caseworkers with a probability calibrated against held-out review outcomes, and the calibration curve and its meaning are published in the caseworker guidance, so a displayed 30 per cent corresponds to roughly 30 in 100 similar claims needing correction.

techniques.name: Temperature Scaling
techniques.description: Temperature scaling is a correction applied after training to a classifier that is more confident than it is accurate, a common problem in modern neural networks. It divides the model's raw scores (logits) by a single number, the temperature, before they are turned into probabilities, so a temperature above one lowers confidence and one below one raises it. The temperature is fitted on a labelled validation set kept apart from training by minimising negative log-likelihood, a measure that penalises confident wrong answers, and the model's own weights are not changed. Because dividing by one positive number never changes which class scores highest, predictions and accuracy stay the same. Stated confidence usually moves much closer to observed accuracy on data like the validation set, which a reliability diagram (a chart of stated confidence against how often the model was right) can show, but some miscalibration remains.

example_use_cases.description: A trust-and-safety team auto-removes posts only when its neural text classifier reports at least 95% confidence. The team fits a temperature on one labelled validation set, then checks on a second, unseen labelled set that posts scored near 95% really are abusive about 95% of the time, and adjusts the removal threshold if they are not.

An environmental agency's land-cover classifier was trained on summer satellite images and is now used on winter scenes, where it is overconfident. The team fits a fresh temperature on a small labelled winter sample and compares calibration error before and after on separate winter test scenes, rather than reusing the summer temperature.

A hospital radiology department displays the model's confidence beside each chest X-ray finding. Before display, the team fits a temperature on held-out scans from its own hospital and reports expected calibration error on a test set, so that clinicians can read a displayed 70% as roughly 70 correct findings in 100 similar cases.

limitations.description: A single temperature is fitted for the whole dataset, so it corrects average overconfidence but not differences between groups or regions of the input space. A minority group can stay overconfident while overall calibration looks good, and only a per-group calibration check shows it.

It leaves predicted classes unchanged, so accuracy and the model's mistakes stay as they were. A weak model remains weak and only becomes more honest about it, so calibration cannot substitute for improving the model.

The temperature is fitted on data resembling the training distribution, and calibration can degrade when deployment data shifts. In one large benchmark, error in stated confidence rose significantly as shift increased, even though it was low on unshifted data.

It needs labelled held-out data that resembles deployment, separate from the training data, and a further separate set to measure the result, because scoring calibration on the data used to fit the temperature flatters it. Small datasets may not leave enough for both.

Calibration is judged on the confidence of the predicted class only. The probabilities given to the other classes are not checked by that measure, so uses that read the whole probability list, such as ranking several likely diagnoses, need separate testing.

resources.title: On Calibration of Modern Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Confidence calibration -- the problem of predicting probability estimates representative of the true correctness likelihood -- is important for classification models in many applications. We discover that modern neural networks, unlike those from a decade ago, are poorly calibrated. Through extensive experiments, we observe that depth, width, weight decay, and Batch Normalization are important factors influencing calibration. We evaluate the performance of various post-processing calibration methods on state-of-the-art architectures with image and document classification datasets. Our analysis and experiments not only offer insights into neural network learning, but also provide a simple and straightforward recipe for practical settings: on most datasets, temperature scaling -- a single-parameter variant of Platt Scaling -- is surprisingly effective at calibrating predictions.

techniques.name: Deep Ensembles
techniques.description: Deep ensembles estimate how uncertain a neural network's predictions are by training several copies of the same network independently and comparing what they predict. Each copy starts from different random initial weights, sees the training data in a different random order, and is trained to output a full predictive distribution, such as a probability for each class or a predicted value with its spread, rather than a single answer. The ensemble's prediction is the average of its members. Where members agree the prediction is usually more reliable, though agreement alone is no guarantee, and where they disagree the model is showing uncertainty about which answer is right, known as epistemic or model uncertainty. In the original study, ensembles of about five networks were better calibrated than single networks, meaning their stated confidence matched how often they were right, and expressed higher uncertainty on inputs from classes absent from the training data.

example_use_cases.description: An autonomous vehicle team runs five independently trained obstacle-detection networks on each camera frame. When the members' outputs disagree beyond a set level, the vehicle slows and requests remote assistance instead of acting on the averaged detection.

A research team estimating body composition from MRI scans trains an ensemble of regression networks that each predict a measurement and its uncertainty, and flags scans where the ensemble is highly uncertain for manual checking before the values enter a population study.

A bank's underwriters see the spread of an ensemble's predicted default probabilities alongside each credit score. Scores with a wide spread are labelled low-confidence and sent for manual review, so staff can see where the model is unsure.

limitations.description: Training and running M networks multiplies compute, memory and latency by roughly M. A five-member ensemble costs about five times a single model, which can rule it out for very large models or for real-time and edge deployment.
Members trained on the same data share its blind spots. On inputs far from the training data they can agree on a confident wrong answer, so low disagreement is not evidence that an input is familiar.

Applies only where the networks can be trained from scratch, with access to the training data and the compute for several full training runs. It cannot be added to an existing pretrained or third-party model.

Disagreement among a small number of members is a noisy estimate, and members that end up too alike understate uncertainty. Calibration has to be checked on held-out data, not assumed from the ensemble.

Uncertainty depends on the training objective and what each member predicts. In regression, variance across member means alone omits the within-member variability included in the original probabilistic method.

resources.title: Simple and Scalable Predictive Uncertainty Estimation using Deep Ensembles
resources.abstract: Deep neural networks (NNs) are powerful black box predictors that have recently achieved impressive performance on a wide spectrum of tasks. Quantifying predictive uncertainty in NNs is a challenging and yet unsolved problem. Bayesian NNs, which learn a distribution over weights, are currently the state-of-the-art for estimating predictive uncertainty; however these require significant modifications to the training procedure and are computationally expensive compared to standard (non-Bayesian) NNs. We propose an alternative to Bayesian NNs that is simple to implement, readily parallelizable, requires very little hyperparameter tuning, and yields high quality predictive uncertainty estimates. Through a series of experiments on classification and regression benchmarks, we demonstrate that our method produces well-calibrated uncertainty estimates which are as good or better than approximate Bayesian NNs. To assess robustness to dataset shift, we evaluate the predictive uncertainty on test examples from known and unknown distributions, and show that our method is able to express higher uncertainty on out-of-distribution examples. We demonstrate the scalability of our method by evaluating predictive uncertainty estimates on ImageNet.
