techniques.name: Monotonicity Constraints
techniques.description: Monotonicity constraints require a model's prediction to move only one way as a chosen input rises, with the other inputs held fixed, so that, for example, predicted salary never falls as years of experience increase. The direction for each constrained feature is set from domain knowledge before training, and the learning algorithm or model structure then rules out any fit that breaks it, so the model cannot learn reversals that come from noise or sampling quirks in the data. Boosted-tree libraries apply the constraint when they choose splits and monotonic neural networks build it into their structure, while penalty-based methods only discourage violations. Because a penalty, a constraint set on the wrong column or a later processing step can still let a reversal through, testers then vary each constrained input across its range over many generated or real cases, with the other inputs fixed, and count any prediction that moves the wrong way. The evidence is that violation count, expected to be zero, together with a comparison of held-out accuracy with and without the constraint.

example_use_cases.description: A mortgage lender constrains its approval model so that higher income, longer employment and a higher credit score can only raise the approval score. Loan officers can then tell an applicant that improving any of these factors can only help the application, and the lender can state each factor's direction to its regulator.

A water utility's pipe-burst risk model is constrained so that risk rises with pipe age and operating pressure and falls with the quality of recent maintenance. Asset managers can then explain the ranked inspection list to the regulator through three directional rules, instead of an opaque score.

A hospital analytics team builds a tree-based model that predicts the cost of care for each patient and constrains the prediction never to fall as age or number of chronic conditions rises. Before release they sweep each constrained feature across its range for thousands of generated patient records, with the other features held fixed, and confirm that no prediction moves the wrong way. They also compare held-out accuracy with and without the constraints.

A utility's day-ahead demand forecast for office buildings is constrained so that predicted demand never falls as occupancy or floor area rises. The validation team writes this as an automated test that draws random building profiles, raises one constrained input at a time and fails the build if any forecast drops, so a retrained model that breaks the rule is caught before deployment.

limitations.description: Forces a one-way relationship even where the real one reverses, such as an inverted U between experience and performance. The model then fits that feature worse and cannot show the turning point, so held-out accuracy should be compared with and without the constraint.

Choosing which features to constrain, and in which direction, needs domain expertise. A wrong constraint builds a false belief into the model, and the check on the trained model will still pass, because it shows only that the constraint holds, not that it is right.

The rule covers one feature with the others held fixed, and says nothing about the size of the effect. A model can meet it by ignoring the feature, and when correlated inputs move together a person's overall score can still fall as one favourable input rises, so the constraint does not make the whole model easy to explain.

Support differs by model family. Tree-boosting libraries such as XGBoost accept constraints directly, while neural networks need a special architecture or a penalty term. With histogram-based tree methods, constraints can remove every candidate split and leave shallow trees that underfit.

A sweep or property-based test samples the input space. It can find a violation but cannot prove there is none, and a pass depends on how well the generated inputs cover realistic and rare combinations of features.

However, when statistical data are used in supervised training of a neural network employing the back‐propagation least mean square algorithm, the behavior of the classification boundary during training is often unpredictable. This research suggests the application of monotonicity constraints to the back propagation learning algorithm. When the training sample set is preprocessed by a linear classification function, neural network performance and efficiency can be improved in classification applications where the feature vector is related monotonically to the pattern vector. Since most classification problems in business possess monotonic properties, this technique is useful in those problems where any assumptions about the properties of the data are inappropriate.

resources.title: An informed monotone neural network for multi-stage chronic kidney disease prediction with integrated GFR estimation
resources.abstract: Chronic kidney disease (CKD) is a progressive condition affecting over 850 million people worldwide, where timely detection and accurate staging are critical to reducing morbidity, mortality, and healthcare burden. Current machine learning approaches often treat CKD prediction as a binary task, neglecting the ordered nature of disease stages, and rarely incorporate physiological constraints or calibrated probability estimates essential for clinical decision support. We propose a multi-stage CKD prediction framework that integrates ordinal classification, probability calibration, and a serum creatinine-monotonicity constraint within a knowledge distillation paradigm. A calibrated CatBoost model serves as a teacher, transferring temperature-scaled class probabilities to an ordinal neural network student augmented with an auxiliary eGFR regression task. Evaluated on a cohort of 750 patients from Al-Ramadi Teaching Hospital, our approach achieved superior macro-F1 and reduced expected calibration error. This work demonstrates that combining ordinal learning, calibration, and physiological constraints yields models that are not only accurate but also aligned with clinical reasoning, offering a pathway toward safer and more trustworthy AI tools for CKD management. Limitations like circular reasoning and target leakage are also discussed.

techniques.name: Generalized Additive Models
techniques.description: A generalised additive model (GAM) builds its prediction by adding a baseline and one smooth curve for each input feature. It extends linear and logistic regression by letting each feature's effect bend, so the model can follow patterns such as risk that climbs steeply after a certain age. Each curve is learned from the data with a smoothing method, such as splines (flexible curves built from joined polynomial pieces). Plotting the curves shows how each feature moves the prediction across its range, so the model can be read directly without a separate explanation method. Because the curves are added together, the model does not capture the joint effect of two features unless a combined term is added by hand.

example_use_cases.description: A hospital builds its 30-day readmission model as a GAM so that its governance committee can audit it. The committee reviews one curve each for age, blood pressure and medication adherence, and queries any stretch where predicted risk falls as a known risk factor rises, since that can point to a data problem rather than a real effect.

A lender uses a GAM for credit scoring so that it can tell a declined applicant how income, credit history and debt-to-income ratio each moved their score. Each factor has its own curve, so the explanation comes straight from the model and needs no separate explanation tool.

An environmental agency models river nitrate levels with a GAM and plots the curve for rainfall. The curve shows the effect levelling off above a certain rainfall, which analysts report to catchment managers instead of a single regression coefficient.

limitations.description: Each feature acts separately, so the model cannot represent effects that depend on two features together, such as the impact of a dose varying with age. Product terms can be added by hand, but each must be thought of in advance and adds a surface that is harder to read than a curve.

The smoothness of each curve is a modelling choice. Cross-validation or penalised fitting selects it automatically, but too little smoothing gives wiggly curves that look like real effects and too much hides genuine bends, so each curve should be read with its confidence band.

When features are strongly related, such as income and age, a nonlinear form of collinearity called concurvity lets one curve absorb part of another's effect. The individual curves can then misstate how much each feature influences the prediction.

A model with dozens of smooth terms produces dozens of curves. Reading them all is slow, so reviewers tend to inspect only the largest effects, and the transparency benefit shrinks as the number of terms grows.
Terms add on the chosen link scale. In a logistic GAM they are contributions to log-odds, not independent additions to readmission probability or guaranteed causal feature effects.

Generalized Additive Models
resources.abstract: Likelihood-based regression models such as the normal linear regression model and the linear logistic model, assume a linear (or some other parametric) form for the covariates X1, X2, …, Xp. We introduce the class of generalized additive models which replaces the linear form Σ βjXj by a sum of smooth functions Σ sj(Xj). The sj(·)'s are unspecified functions that are estimated using a scatterplot smoother, in an iterative procedure we call the local scoring algorithm. The technique is applicable to any likelihood-based regression model: the class of generalized linear models contains many of these. In this class the linear predictor η = Σ βjXj is replaced by the additive predictor Σ sj(Xj); hence, the name generalized additive models. We illustrate the technique with binary response and survival data. In both cases, the method proves to be useful in uncovering nonlinear covariate effects. It has the advantage of being completely automatic, i.e., no "detective work" is needed on the part of the statistician. As a theoretical underpinning, the technique is viewed as an empirical method of maximizing the expected log likelihood, or equivalently, of minimizing the Kullback-Leibler distance to the true model.

resources.title: Fast Stable Restricted Maximum Likelihood and Marginal Likelihood Estimation of Semiparametric Generalized Linear Models
resources.abstract: Recent work by Reiss and Ogden provides a theoretical basis for sometimes preferring restricted maximum likelihood (REML) to generalized cross-validation (GCV) for smoothing parameter selection in semiparametric regression. However, existing REML or marginal likelihood (ML) based methods for semiparametric generalized linear models (GLMs) use iterative REML or ML estimation of the smoothing parameters of working linear approximations to the GLM. Such indirect schemes need not converge and fail to do so in a non-negligible proportion of practical analyses. By contrast, very reliable prediction error criteria smoothing parameter selection methods are available, based on direct optimization of GCV, or related criteria, for the GLM itself. Since such methods directly optimize properly defined functions of the smoothing parameters, they have much more reliable convergence properties. The paper develops the first such method for REML or ML estimation of smoothing parameters. A Laplace approximation is used to obtain an approximate REML or ML for any GLM, which is suitable for efficient direct optimization. This REML or ML criterion requires that Newton–Raphson iteration, rather than Fisher scoring, be used for GLM fitting, and a computationally stable approach to this is proposed. The REML or ML criterion itself is optimized by a Newton method, with the derivatives required obtained by a mixture of implicit differentiation and direct methods. The method will cope with numerical rank deficiency in the fitted model and in fact provides a slight improvement in numerical robustness on the earlier method of Wood for prediction error criteria based smoothness selection. Simulation results suggest that the new REML and ML methods offer some improvement in mean-square error performance relative to GCV or Akaike’s information criterion in most cases, without the small number of severe undersmoothing failures to which Akaike’s information criterion and GCV are prone. This is achieved at the same computational cost as GCV or Akaike’s information criterion. The new approach also eliminates the convergence failures of previous REML- or ML-based approaches for penalized GLMs and usually has lower computational cost than these alternatives. Example applications are presented in adaptive smoothing, scalar on function regression and generalized additive model selection.

Intelligible Models for HealthCare
resources.abstract: In machine learning often a tradeoff must be made between accuracy and intelligibility. More accurate models such as boosted trees, random forests, and neural nets usually are not intelligible, but more intelligible models such as logistic regression, naive-Bayes, and single decision trees often have significantly worse accuracy. This tradeoff sometimes limits the accuracy of models that can be applied in mission-critical applications such as healthcare where being able to understand, validate, edit, and trust a learned model is important. We present two case studies where high-performance generalized additive models with pairwise interactions (GA2Ms) are applied to real healthcare problems yielding intelligible models with state-of-the-art accuracy. In the pneumonia risk prediction case study, the intelligible model uncovers surprising patterns in the data that previously had prevented complex learned models from being fielded in this domain, but because it is intelligible and modular allows these patterns to be recognized and removed. In the 30-day hospital readmission case study, we show that the same methods scale to large datasets containing hundreds of thousands of patients and thousands of attributes while remaining intelligible and providing accuracy comparable to the best (unintelligible) machine learning methods.

sample_claims.text: Every input to the readmission risk model acts through a single plotted curve, so a clinician can read off how predicted risk changes with each input without running a separate explanation method.
The direction of each applicant attribute's effect in the credit model, as plotted with its confidence band, matches what credit risk specialists expect, and any departure has been explained.
The resource allocation model's score for any case is a baseline plus one contribution per policy factor, so each factor's share of a decision can be stated and audited.
Each nonlinear effect the model reports departs from a straight line by more than the width of its confidence band, so the bend is not an artefact of over-flexible smoothing.

techniques.name: Concept Activation Vectors
techniques.description: A concept activation vector (CAV) is a direction inside a neural network that stands for a human idea such as 'stripes'. The analyst supplies example inputs showing the concept and random counter-examples, and trains a simple linear classifier to separate the network's activations (the values a chosen layer produces) for the two sets. The CAV is the direction at right angles to that classifier's dividing boundary, pointing towards the concept examples. Testing with CAVs (TCAV) then reports, for one output class, the share of its inputs whose class score would rise if the activations moved in the concept's direction, and repeating this with many random counter-example sets and applying a significance test guards against a meaningless direction. Concept sets built from examples of a protected characteristic, such as gender or ethnicity, turn the test into a check of whether a class is sensitive to that characteristic, as the original paper demonstrates.

example_use_cases.description: Auditing a medical imaging model to check whether its chest X-ray classifications are sensitive to diagnostic concepts (like 'tumour characteristics') or to irrelevant ones (like 'scanner type' or 'patient positioning'), so the clinical team can judge whether the model relies on medically relevant information.

A team auditing an image classifier used for content tagging builds concept sets from photographs of people of different ethnicities and genders, with random photographs as the comparison, and tests each output class for significant sensitivity to those concepts, as the original paper did. Classes with significant sensitivity to an ethnicity or gender concept are listed for retraining with balanced data; a low score is not taken as clearance.

A developer of a driver-assistance system documents, for a type-approval authority, how its traffic-sign classifier responds to visual concepts. The report gives significance-tested TCAV scores for the 'stop sign' class against concepts such as graffiti, snow cover and low sun glare, so the authority can see what the classifier's predictions are sensitive to.

limitations.description: Requires clearly defined concept examples and non-concept examples, which can be hard to obtain for abstract or subjective concepts. If the examples differ from the random counter-examples in other ways, such as image source or lighting, the CAV mixes those differences in with the concept.

Assumes the concept is represented as a direction that a linear classifier can pick out at the chosen layer. If the concept is not linearly separable there, the CAV is unreliable, so check that the classifier separates the two sets well before reading any scores.

Results depend heavily on which layer is examined, because layers capture different levels of abstraction. A concept can be invisible at one layer and strong at another, so a single-layer result should not be generalised.

The significance test trains hundreds of classifiers per concept and layer (the paper uses about 500), so cost multiplies with the number of concepts and layers tested. FastCAV, a 2025 preprint, reports speed-ups of up to 63.6 times.

Scores are class-level and describe sensitivity, not cause. A TCAV score is the share of a class's inputs whose score rises along the concept direction, so it does not explain an individual decision, and a high score does not show that the concept causes the prediction.

resources.title: FastCAV: Efficient Computation of Concept Activation Vectors for Explaining Deep Neural Networks
resources.abstract: Concepts such as objects, patterns, and shapes are how humans understand the world. Building on this intuition, concept-based explainability methods aim to study representations learned by deep neural networks in relation to human-understandable concepts. Here, Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs) are an important tool and can identify whether a model learned a concept or not. However, the computational cost and time requirements of existing CAV computation pose a significant challenge, particularly in large-scale, high-dimensional architectures. To address this limitation, we introduce FastCAV, a novel approach that accelerates the extraction of CAVs by up to 63.6x (on average 46.4x). We provide a theoretical foundation for our approach and give concrete assumptions under which it is equivalent to established SVM-based methods. Our empirical results demonstrate that CAVs calculated with FastCAV maintain similar performance while being more efficient and stable. In downstream applications, i.e., concept-based explanation methods, we show that FastCAV can act as a replacement leading to equivalent insights. Hence, our approach enables previously infeasible investigations of deep models, which we demonstrate by tracking the evolution of concepts during model training.

resources.title: Interpretability Beyond Feature Attribution: Quantitative Testing with Concept Activation Vectors (TCAV)
resources.abstract: The interpretation of deep learning models is a challenge due to their size, complexity, and often opaque internal state. In addition, many systems, such as image classifiers, operate on low-level features rather than high-level concepts. To address these challenges, we introduce Concept Activation Vectors (CAVs), which provide an interpretation of a neural net’s internal state in terms of human-friendly concepts. The key idea is to view the high-dimensional internal state of a neural net as an aid, not an obstacle. We show how to use CAVs as part of a technique, Testing with CAVs (TCAV), that uses directional derivatives to quantify the degree to which a user-defined concept is important to a classification result–for example, how sensitive a prediction of “zebra” is to the presence of stripes. Using the domain of image classification as a testing ground, we describe how CAVs may be used to explore hypotheses and generate insights for a standard image classification network as well as a medical application.

resources.title: Global and Local Interpretability for Cardiac MRI Classification
resources.abstract: Deep learning methods for classifying medical images have demonstrated impressive accuracy in a wide range of tasks but often these models are hard to interpret, limiting their applicability in clinical practice. In this work we introduce a convolutional neural network model for identifying disease in temporal sequences of cardiac MR segmentations which is interpretable in terms of clinically familiar measurements. The model is based around a variational autoencoder, reducing the input into a low-dimensional latent space in which classification occurs. We then use the recently developed `concept activation vector' technique to associate concepts which are diagnostically meaningful (eg. clinical biomarkers such as `low left-ventricular ejection fraction') to certain vectors in the latent space. These concepts are then qualitatively inspected by observing the change in the image domain resulting from interpolations in the latent space in the direction of these vectors. As a result, when the model classifies images it is also capable of providing naturally interpretable concepts relevant to that classification and demonstrating the meaning of those concepts in the image domain. Our approach is demonstrated on the UK Biobank cardiac MRI dataset where we detect the presence of coronary artery disease.

resources.title: Concept attribution: Explaining CNN decisions to physicians
resources.abstract: Deep learning explainability is often reached by gradient-based approaches that attribute the network output to perturbations of the input pixels. However, the relevance of input pixels may be difficult to relate to relevant image features in some applications, e.g. diagnostic measures in medical imaging. The framework described in this paper shifts the attribution focus from pixel values to user-defined concepts. By checking if certain diagnostic measures are present in the learned representations, experts can explain and entrust the network output. Being post-hoc, our method does not alter the network training and can be easily plugged into the latest state-of-the-art convolutional networks. This paper presents the main components of the framework for attribution to concepts, in addition to the introduction of a spatial pooling operation on top of the feature maps to obtain a solid interpretability analysis. Furthermore, regularized regression is analyzed as a solution to the regression overfitting in high-dimensionality latent spaces. The versatility of the proposed approach is shown by experiments on two medical applications, namely histopathology and retinopathy, and on one non-medical task, the task of handwritten digit classification. The obtained explanations are in line with clinicians' guidelines and complementary to widely used visualization tools such as saliency maps.

sample_claims.text: The chest X-ray classifier's 'pneumonia' predictions are significantly sensitive to clinically recognised findings and not significantly sensitive to scanner type or patient positioning, at the layers tested.

The content-tagging classifier's TCAV scores for the ethnicity and gender concept sets are recorded for every output class at the tested layers, and the classes with significant sensitivity are listed for review.
The traffic-sign classifier's sensitivity to graffiti, snow cover and glare concepts is documented with significance-tested TCAV scores for each sign class the approval authority has requested.
The object recogniser's class predictions depend mainly on concepts that domain experts regard as meaningful for that class, such as shape and texture, rather than on background concepts.

techniques.name: API Usage Pattern Monitoring
techniques.description: API usage pattern monitoring examines how each account uses a deployed model's API, to catch misuse that no single request reveals. The monitor keeps a running record per account and compares it with a baseline of normal use, raising an alert when the account departs from it. Published detectors for model theft show two ways to do this: one tests whether the distances between an account's successive queries follow the bell-shaped pattern that ordinary use produces, and another estimates how much of the model's behaviour the account's queries and responses would let someone rebuild. Providers also score how often an account triggers content filters or repeats jailbreak attempts, and send high scores for review. The output is a log of alerts and the actions taken, which gives a dated record of how the API was used compared with the uses it was approved for.

example_use_cases.description: A fraud-scoring API provider examines each client's query stream for runs of near-identical transactions altered in small steps, which suggest someone is probing for the score at which a transaction passes. Flagged accounts are rate-limited and sent to the security team for review.

A company selling traffic-sign recognition as a paid API tests whether the spacing between each customer's successive image queries follows the pattern ordinary use produces. Accounts whose queries look synthetic and widely spread, as in model-copying attacks, are flagged for investigation and possible suspension.

A health-technology company serving a paediatric triage model to many clinics monitors each clinic's query volumes and the ages in its requests. A clinic sending mostly adult patients, or a sudden change after a software update, is flagged so the company can contact it before unsafe advice is given.

A provider of a text-generation API scores each customer's usage by how often prompts and responses are flagged as harmful and whether jailbreak attempts recur. Customers with high scores go to review, which can lead to a warning or suspension.

A bank's model risk team compares the monthly log of calls to its credit-scoring API, by internal team and purpose, with the uses approved at validation. The comparison is filed in the model's audit record, so reviewers can see whether the model is used as documented.

limitations.description: Anomalies are defined against a baseline of normal use, and ordinary users can be unusual. In PRADA's tests, legitimate queries made of consecutive frames from a sequence triggered false alarms at stricter settings, so the alert threshold has to be tuned to each model and use case.

A patient attacker can stay inside normal limits by querying slowly, adding dummy queries or spreading queries across many accounts. PRADA's authors show that padding queries raises the attacker's cost three to ten times, and that multiple accounts defeat per-account analysis.

Useful monitoring needs request content, or features of it, to be logged and sometimes read by reviewers. For sensitive applications that may be unlawful or unacceptable, and Microsoft notes that detection may be less accurate when human review is switched off for such customers.

Detectors keep state for every account. PRADA's authors estimate a few gigabytes in total for a few hundred clients of an image model, and the cost rises with traffic and with the retention period set for audit evidence.

The published extraction detectors were tested on small models, decision trees in one case and image classifiers in the other, against simulated attackers. Kesarwani et al. describe their warning as approximate, so an alert is a lead for investigation, not proof of theft.

resources.title: Model Extraction Warning in MLaaS Paradigm
resources.abstract: Machine learning models deployed on the cloud are susceptible to several security threats including extraction attacks. Adversaries may abuse a model's prediction API to steal the model thus compromising model confidentiality, privacy of training data, and revenue from future query payments. This work introduces a model extraction monitor that quantifies the extraction status of models by continually observing the API query and response streams of users. We present two novel strategies that measure either the information gain or the coverage of the feature space spanned by user queries to estimate the learning rate of individual and colluding adversaries. Both approaches have low computational overhead and can easily be offered as services to model owners to warn them against state of the art extraction attacks. We demonstrate empirical performance results of these approaches for decision tree and neural network models using open source datasets and BigML MLaaS platform.

resources.title: PRADA: Protecting Against DNN Model Stealing Attacks
resources.abstract: Machine learning (ML) applications are increasingly prevalent. Protecting the confidentiality of ML models becomes paramount for two reasons: (a) a model can be a business advantage to its owner, and (b) an adversary may use a stolen model to find transferable adversarial examples that can evade classification by the original model. Access to the model can be restricted to be only via well-defined prediction APIs. Nevertheless, prediction APIs still provide enough information to allow an adversary to mount model extraction attacks by sending repeated queries via the prediction API. In this paper, we describe new model extraction attacks using novel approaches for generating synthetic queries, and optimizing training hyperparameters. Our attacks outperform state-of-the-art model extraction in terms of transferability of both targeted and non-targeted adversarial examples (up to +29-44 percentage points, pp), and prediction accuracy (up to +46 pp) on two datasets. We provide take-aways on how to perform effective model extraction attacks. We then propose PRADA, the first step towards generic and effective detection of DNN model extraction attacks. It analyzes the distribution of consecutive API queries and raises an alarm when this distribution deviates from benign behavior. We show that PRADA can detect all prior model extraction attacks with no false positives.

sample_claims.text: The fraud API logs alerts from the configured query-distance detector so the security team can investigate suspected extraction-style sequences.
The clinical assistant records recurring harmful-content classifier flags by frequency and severity for the stated monitoring period.

The moderation API records recurring harmful-content signals and the resulting safety-review alerts.

techniques.name: Knowledge Boundary Probing
techniques.description: Knowledge boundary probing maps what a language model can and cannot reliably answer. A probe set is built from questions across the topics the system will face, including some with known answers and some that cannot be answered. Each question is asked in several phrasings, because a model may answer one wording correctly and fail on another. Responses are scored for correctness, for whether the model signals doubt when it should, and for whether its stated or computed confidence tracks whether it is right. The result is a topic-by-topic map of what the model knows, knows only under some phrasings, and does not know, which informs where to deploy it, what to tell users about its limits, and where to add training data or human review.

example_use_cases.description: A government analytics team using an LLM to summarise policy evidence probes it on well-researched areas and on recent or local policy it cannot have seen in training. Accuracy drops on the second group, so the team adds a retrieval step for those topics before the tool is used in briefings.

A bank adds a per-topic table of probe results (accurate on card fees, weak on mortgage rules) to the model documentation for its customer-service chatbot. The app uses the table to tell customers when to check with an adviser.

A school-software vendor checks an LLM maths tutor against each curriculum unit, asking every question in several wordings. Units where correctness changes with the wording are marked for teacher review instead of being shown to students unsupervised.

limitations.description: The probe set samples a finite number of topics and question types. A clean result on those says little about topics the set omits, so the map is only as broad as the probes, and mapping every domain is infeasible.

Whether a model 'knows' something depends on how the question is worded. A single phrasing can understate or overstate what the model knows, so each question needs several phrasings, and the boundary is fuzzy rather than a clean line.

Models can be confidently wrong, and can hedge on things they know, so stated or computed confidence is only a rough guide to knowledge. Calibration also varies by topic, so one overall score can hide weak areas.

Scoring needs labelled questions and a way to detect hedging. Deciding which questions are truly unanswerable takes human judgement, and detectors built on one model's uncertainty phrases may miss how other models express doubt.
The map holds for one model version. Fine-tuning, a model update or added retrieval shifts the boundary, so the probes must be rerun after each change to keep the map accurate.

Benchmarking Knowledge Boundary for Large Language Models: A Different Perspective on Model Evaluation
resources.abstract: In recent years, substantial advancements have been made in the development of large language models, achieving remarkable performance across diverse tasks. To evaluate the knowledge ability of language models, previous studies have proposed lots of benchmarks based on question-answering pairs. We argue that it is not reliable and comprehensive to evaluate language models with a fixed question or limited paraphrases as the query, since language models are sensitive to prompt. Therefore, we introduce a novel concept named knowledge boundary to encompass both prompt-agnostic and prompt-sensitive knowledge within language models. Knowledge boundary avoids prompt sensitivity in language model evaluations, rendering them more dependable and robust. To explore the knowledge boundary for a given model, we propose projected gradient descent method with semantic constraints, a new algorithm designed to identify the optimal prompt for each piece of knowledge. Experiments demonstrate a superior performance of our algorithm in computing the knowledge boundary compared to existing methods. Furthermore, we evaluate the ability of multiple language models in several domains with knowledge boundary.

resources.title: Do Large Language Models Know What They Don’t Know?
resources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have a wealth of knowledge that allows them to excel in various Natural Language Processing (NLP) tasks.Current research focuses on enhancing their performance within their existing knowledge.Despite their vast knowledge, LLMs are still limited by the amount of information they can accommodate and comprehend.Therefore, the ability to understand their own limitations on the unknows, referred to as self-knowledge, is of paramount importance.This study aims to evaluate LLMs' self-knowledge by assessing their ability to identify unanswerable or unknowable questions.We introduce an automated methodology to detect uncertainty in the responses of these models, providing a novel measure of their self-knowledge.We further introduce a unique dataset, SelfAware, consisting of unanswerable questions from five diverse categories and their answerable counterparts.Our extensive analysis, involving 20 LLMs including GPT-3, InstructGPT, and LLaMA, discovering an intrinsic capacity for self-knowledge within these models.Moreover, we demonstrate that in-context learning and instruction tuning can further enhance this self-knowledge.Despite this promising insight, our findings also highlight a considerable gap between the capabilities of these models and human proficiency in recognizing the limits of their knowledge. "True wisdom is knowing what you don't know." -Confucius

resources.title: Aleatoric and epistemic uncertainty in machine learning: an introduction to concepts and methods
resources.abstract: The notion of uncertainty is of major importance in machine learning and constitutes a key element of machine learning methodology. In line with the statistical tradition, uncertainty has long been perceived as almost synonymous with standard probability and probabilistic predictions. Yet, due to the steadily increasing relevance of machine learning for practical applications and related issues such as safety requirements, new problems and challenges have recently been identified by machine learning scholars, and these problems may call for new methodological developments. In particular, this includes the importance of distinguishing between (at least) two different types of uncertainty, often referred to as aleatoric and epistemic . In this paper, we provide an introduction to the topic of uncertainty in machine learning as well as an overview of attempts so far at handling uncertainty in general and formalizing this distinction in particular.

Calibration of Self-Reported Confidence and Accuracy of Large Language Models in Medical Question Answering
resources.abstract: Objective: To evaluate the alignment between self-reported confidence of large language models (LLM) and their accuracy in answering medical multiple-choice questions. Materials and Methods: We prompted six LLMs (GPT-5, GPT-5-mini, GPT-5-nano, GPT-4o, Claude Sonnet 4.5, and Gemini 2.5) to answer MedMCQA items and report confidence scores. Based on 12,000 LLM responses, we calculated Expected Calibration Errors (ECE) by averaging absolute differences between observed accuracy and predicted confidence. Results: Mean ECE differed by model (Claude Sonnet 4.5 best: 0.06; Gpt-4o worst: 0.127) and varied across specialties (“Skin” best: 0.041; “Social & Preventive Medicine” worst: 0.141). Accuracy of examined LLMs showed analogous variation between specialties. Discussion: Our results demonstrate that high accuracy does not guarantee reliable uncertainty estimation. We identified substantial heterogeneity across medical specialties, where pooled metrics masked a threefold ECE increase between best- and worst-performing domains. Conclusion: We recommend incorporating calibration reporting into LLM evaluations, as larger models exhibit improved “self-knowledge”, but uneven overconfidence persists.

techniques.name: Machine Unlearning
techniques.description: Machine unlearning removes the influence of specific training records from a trained model, so that the model behaves as if it had never seen them. It is used when someone withdraws consent or asks for deletion, for example under the right to erasure (the 'right to be forgotten') in data protection law, and retraining from scratch would be too slow or costly. Exact methods, such as sharded training, split the data into parts that each train their own sub-model, so a deletion means retraining only the sub-model that used those records, which gives a result statistically the same as retraining without them. Approximate methods instead edit the trained model directly to reduce the records' influence, which is faster but gives weaker assurance, and certified methods add a formal bound on how much influence can remain.

example_use_cases.description: A social media platform responds to a user's deletion request by removing that user's interaction history from its recommendation model, retraining only the affected part rather than the whole system. The data protection team uses this to decide whether it can meet deletion deadlines without a full retrain each time.

A hospital withdraws a patient's records from a readmission-risk model after the patient withdraws consent for research use, retraining only the shard that contained them. The research governance board uses the retraining log to decide whether the model can stay in use.

A lender removes a former customer's transaction history from its credit-risk model after the customer withdraws consent for analytics use. The model risk team decides whether a faster approximate update is acceptable or whether the affected shard must be retrained exactly.

A financial institution records the withdrawn transaction-record identifiers, affected constituent models and retraining checkpoints in its SISA workflow. Reviewers use this update history to inspect the scope of the completed unlearning operation.

limitations.description: Exact unlearning for deep neural networks gives limited savings over full retraining: sharded training sped unlearning up by only 1.36 times on ImageNet-scale classification in the SISA paper. For very large foundation models, even storing the checkpoints needed for partial retraining can be infeasible, which limits exact methods to smaller models.

Approximate methods can leave residual influence from the removed data in the model, and their guarantees are weaker or only probabilistic. That matters when a regulator or the data subject expects genuine erasure, because the result cannot be shown to match a model retrained without the data.

Unlearning is hard to verify from outside. There is no direct way to measure one record's influence on a model's weights, so the data subject must largely trust the provider's procedure, and membership inference tests can detect leakage but cannot prove removal.

Removing many records, or records the model relies on, can lower accuracy, and sharded exact methods lose accuracy because each sub-model sees only part of the data, most on complex tasks. Teams with frequent deletion requests need to monitor accuracy after each round.

Exact approaches such as sharded training must be built into the training pipeline before the model is first trained, and most methods need white-box access to weights and training data. A model already trained without them, or a third-party model, can only be retrained or approximately edited.

resources.title: Digital forgetting in large language models: A survey of unlearning methods
resources.abstract: Large language models (LLMs) have become the state of the art in natural language processing. The massive adoption of generative LLMs and the capabilities they have shown have prompted public concerns regarding their impact on the labor market, privacy, the use of copyrighted work, and how these models align with human ethics and the rule of law. As a response, new regulations are being pushed, which require developers and service providers to evaluate, monitor, and forestall or at least mitigate the risks posed by their models. One mitigation strategy is digital forgetting: given a model with undesirable knowledge or behavior, the goal is to obtain a new model where the detected issues are no longer present. Digital forgetting is usually enforced via machine unlearning techniques, which modify trained machine learning models for them to behave as models trained on a subset of the original training data. In this work, we describe the motivations and desirable properties of digital forgetting when applied to LLMs, and we survey recent works on machine unlearning. Specifically, we propose a taxonomy of unlearning methods based on the reach and depth of the modifications done on the models, we discuss and compare the effectiveness of machine unlearning methods for LLMs proposed so far, and we survey their evaluation. Finally, we describe open problems of machine unlearning applied to LLMs and we put forward recommendations for developers and practitioners.

resources.title: Towards Making Systems Forget with Machine Unlearning
resources.abstract: Today's systems produce a rapidly exploding amount of data, and the data further derives more data, forming a complex data propagation network that we call the data's lineage. There are many reasons that users want systems to forget certain data including its lineage. From a privacy perspective, users who become concerned with new privacy risks of a system often want the system to forget their data and lineage. From a security perspective, if an attacker pollutes an anomaly detector by injecting manually crafted data into the training data set, the detector must forget the injected data to regain security. From a usability perspective, a user can remove noise and incorrect entries so that a recommendation engine gives useful recommendations. Therefore, we envision forgetting systems, capable of forgetting certain data and their lineages, completely and quickly. This paper focuses on making learning systems forget, the process of which we call machine unlearning, or simply unlearning. We present a general, efficient unlearning approach by transforming learning algorithms used by a system into a summation form. To forget a training data sample, our approach simply updates a small number of summations -- asymptotically faster than retraining from scratch. Our approach is general, because the summation form is from the statistical query learning in which many machine learning algorithms can be implemented. Our approach also applies to all stages of machine learning, including feature selection and modeling. Our evaluation, on four diverse learning systems and real-world workloads, shows that our approach is general, effective, fast, and easy to use.

resources.title: Machine Unlearning
resources.abstract: Once users have shared their data online, it is generally difficult for them to revoke access and ask for the data to be deleted. Machine learning (ML) exacerbates this problem because any model trained with said data may have memorized it, putting users at risk of a successful privacy attack exposing their information. Yet, having models unlearn is notoriously difficult.We introduce SISA training, a framework that expedites the unlearning process by strategically limiting the influence of a data point in the training procedure. While our framework is applicable to any learning algorithm, it is designed to achieve the largest improvements for stateful algorithms like stochastic gradient descent for deep neural networks. SISA training reduces the computational overhead associated with unlearning, even in the worst-case setting where unlearning requests are made uniformly across the training set. In some cases, the service provider may have a prior on the distribution of unlearning requests that will be issued by users. We may take this prior into account to partition and order data accordingly, and further decrease overhead from unlearning.Our evaluation spans several datasets from different domains, with corresponding motivations for unlearning. Under no distributional assumptions, for simple learning tasks, we observe that SISA training improves time to unlearn points from the Purchase dataset by 4.63×, and 2.45× for the SVHN dataset, over retraining from scratch. SISA training also provides a speed-up of 1.36× in retraining for complex learning tasks such as ImageNet classification; aided by transfer learning, this results in a small degradation in accuracy. Our work contributes to practical data governance in machine unlearning.

From the perspective of utility, if a system’s utility is damaged by some bad data, the system needs to forget such data to regain utility. While unlearning is very important, it has not been well-considered in existing recommender systems. Although there are some researches have studied the problem of machine unlearning, existing methods can not be directly applied to recommendation as they are unable to consider the collaborative information.

techniques.name: Out-of-Domain Detection
techniques.description: Out-of-domain detection checks whether a user's query falls inside the topics and tasks a conversational AI system is meant to handle. Scope is defined by examples, such as an assistant's supported intents (the actions it can recognise), and a detector then scores how closely each new query resembles them. Typical detectors set a minimum confidence on an intent classifier, add an explicit out-of-scope class trained on examples of unsupported queries, or measure how far a query's embedding, a numerical summary of its meaning, lies from the in-scope examples. A query judged out of scope can be declined, handed to a person or another service, or answered with a request to rephrase, instead of receiving an unreliable or invented answer. The detector tests resemblance to the defined scope, not what the system actually knows, so it needs evaluating on realistic out-of-scope queries.

example_use_cases.description: Enabling a medical chatbot specialised in diabetes management to recognise and deflect questions about unrelated conditions, avoiding potentially dangerous medical advice outside its training domain.

Ensuring an educational AI tutor for high school mathematics reliably identifies advanced university-level questions and redirects students to appropriate resources rather than attempting explanations beyond its scope.

An insurer's claims-intake assistant is built for routine motor and household claims. Messages about unfamiliar claim types, such as large flood events or commercial losses, are detected and routed to a specialist adjuster instead of being handled with irrelevant questions.

A council's resident-services chatbot covers bin collections, parking permits and council tax. When a resident asks about something it does not cover, such as a planning dispute, it says so, names the service that can help and logs the query, and the log shows the council which topics residents ask about that the chatbot cannot answer.

limitations.description: Scope has to be defined before it can be detected, and general-purpose assistants or fuzzy domains have no clean edge. A narrow definition refuses legitimate queries, and a loose one lets unsupported queries through.

Detection is weakest on queries that resemble in-scope ones. In the 2019 benchmark that introduced the task, no intent classifier caught more than about two-thirds of out-of-scope queries even when trained on examples of them, so recall should be measured on realistic out-of-scope queries before the detector is relied on.
The threshold trades wrongly refusing valid queries against wrongly answering unsupported ones. The two errors rarely cost the same, and queries near the boundary will still land on both sides.
Users can rephrase or disguise an unsupported request so that it resembles in-scope wording. A detector tested only on plain phrasings overstates how well it holds up against paraphrase.

Scope changes as capabilities are added or retired, so the detector and its out-of-scope test set need refreshing, or it will refuse newly supported queries and accept newly unsupported ones. Building realistic out-of-scope examples is costly because annotators need expert knowledge of the in-scope intents.

resources.title: An Evaluation Dataset for Intent Classification and Out-of-Scope Prediction
resources.abstract: Task-oriented dialog systems need to know when a query falls outside their range of supported intents, but current text classification corpora only define label sets that cover every example. We introduce a new dataset that includes queries that are out-of-scope—i.e., queries that do not fall into any of the system’s supported intents. This poses a new challenge because models cannot assume that every query at inference time belongs to a system-supported intent class. Our dataset also covers 150 intent classes over 10 domains, capturing the breadth that a production task-oriented agent must handle. We evaluate a range of benchmark classifiers on our dataset along with several different out-of-scope identification schemes. We find that while the classifiers perform well on in-scope intent classification, they struggle to identify out-of-scope queries. Our dataset and evaluation fill an important gap in the field, offering a way of more rigorously and realistically benchmarking text classification in task-driven dialog systems.

techniques.name: Isotonic Regression Calibration
techniques.description: Isotonic regression calibration turns a classifier's scores into calibrated probabilities by fitting a step-shaped function that never decreases as the score rises. Unlike a fixed curve, it assumes nothing about the shape of the miscalibration except that a higher score should never mean a lower chance of the positive outcome, so it can correct any distortion that leaves the cases in the right order. It is fitted on labelled cases the classifier was not trained on: the cases are sorted by score, and the pool-adjacent-violators algorithm repeatedly merges neighbouring groups whose observed positive rates are out of order, until the rates rise steadily with the score. Each merged group's observed rate becomes the calibrated probability for scores in its range, and the result is assessed with a reliability diagram (predicted probability plotted against observed frequency) and the Brier score (a measure of how far predicted probabilities fall from what happened) before and after.

example_use_cases.description: A clinical research team builds a random forest on electronic health records to predict which adolescents will attempt suicide. The forest ranks patients well, but its vote shares are not probabilities, so the team fits isotonic regression on held-out records and reports calibration slope, intercept and Brier score before the risk estimates are used to prioritise clinical follow-up.

An insurer's pricing team applies isotonic recalibration to the output of its claim-probability model, fitted on a large portfolio and checked on a later year of policies, so that within each band of predicted risk the average prediction matches the observed claim rate and no price band systematically subsidises another.

An online marketplace scores listings for fraud with a naive Bayes text classifier whose probabilities cluster near 0 and 1, and analysts had been treating them as near-certainties. With tens of thousands of labelled past cases available, the team fits isotonic calibration so the review queue shows probabilities that match observed fraud rates, and shares the reliability diagram with the analysts.

limitations.description: It needs plenty of calibration data. With fewer than about a thousand labelled cases the step function follows noise in the calibration set. Because each step matches the observed rate exactly on the cases it was fitted to, calibration checked on those same cases looks perfect whatever its true quality, so it must be checked on separate cases. The two-parameter curve of Platt scaling usually does as well or better on small sets; isotonic regression pays off when calibration data are plentiful.

The output is a step function, so many different scores receive exactly the same probability. These ties discard distinctions the model made within a step, can change ranking measures such as the area under the ROC curve after calibration, and matter when a decision threshold falls inside a wide step.

It relies on the classifier's ordering being right: a higher score must never mean a lower chance of the outcome. Where the model ranks cases wrongly over some range of scores, isotonic regression cannot repair the ranking and instead flattens that range into a single probability.

Probabilities at the extremes rest on little data. The outermost steps can be fitted from a handful of cases and may sit at or near 0 or 1, and common implementations clip scores beyond the range seen in calibration to the end values, so the most extreme predictions are the least trustworthy.

Previous calibration methods apply only to two-class problems. Here, we show how to obtain accurate probability estimates for multiclass problems by combining calibrated binary probability estimates. We also propose a new method for obtaining calibrated two-class probability estimates that can be applied to any classifier that produces a ranking of examples. Using naive Bayes and support vector machine classifiers, we give experimental results from a variety of two-class and multiclass domains, including direct marketing, text categorization and digit recognition.

resources.title: Predicting suicide attempts in adolescents with longitudinal clinical data and machine learning
resources.abstract: Background Adolescents have high rates of nonfatal suicide attempts, but clinically practical risk prediction remains a challenge. Screening can be time consuming to implement at scale, if it is done at all. Computational algorithms may predict suicide risk using only routinely collected clinical data. We used a machine learning approach validated on longitudinal clinical data in adults to address this challenge in adolescents. Methods This is a retrospective, longitudinal cohort study. Data were collected from the Vanderbilt Synthetic Derivative from January 1998 to December 2015 and included 974 adolescents with nonfatal suicide attempts and multiple control comparisons: 496 adolescents with other self‐injury ( OSI ), 7,059 adolescents with depressive symptoms, and 25,081 adolescent general hospital controls. Candidate predictors included diagnostic, demographic, medication, and socioeconomic factors. Outcome was determined by multiexpert review of electronic health records. Random forests were validated with optimism adjustment at multiple time points (from 1 week to 2 years). Recalibration was done via isotonic regression. Evaluation metrics included discrimination ( AUC , sensitivity/specificity, precision/recall) and calibration (calibration plots, slope/intercept, Brier score). Results Computational models performed well and did not require face‐to‐face screening. Performance improved as suicide attempts became more imminent. Discrimination was good in comparison with OSI controls ( AUC = 0.83 [0.82–0.84] at 720 days; AUC = 0.85 [0.84–0.87] at 7 days) and depressed controls ( AUC = 0.87 [95% CI 0.85–0.90] at 720 days; 0.90 [0.85–0.94] at 7 days) and best in comparison with general hospital controls ( AUC 0.94 [0.92–0.96] at 720 days; 0.97 [0.95–0.98] at 7 days). Random forests significantly outperformed logistic regression in every comparison. Recalibration improved performance as much as ninefold – clinical recommendations with poorly calibrated predictions can lead to decision errors. Conclusions Machine learning on longitudinal clinical data may provide a scalable approach to broaden screening for risk of nonfatal suicide attempts in adolescents.

techniques.name: CycloneDX Machine Learning Bill of Materials
techniques.description: A CycloneDX ML-BOM (machine-learning bill of materials) is a machine-readable inventory of what a model is made of, written in the CycloneDX standard (ECMA-424) so that tools as well as people can check it. It applies the software bill of materials, a structured list of the components in a piece of software, to models: the model is declared as a component of type machine-learning-model with its identifiers, version, supplier, licence and file hashes, together with the base models it was derived from (its pedigree), the datasets used to train and evaluate it with their source, classification and owners, the libraries it depends on, and an optional structured model card giving its task, architecture, performance metrics, intended uses and known limitations. The BOM is written at release, by hand or with a generator that reads the model's repository and metadata, checked against the CycloneDX schema, and can be signed. Consumers then query it, for example to find every deployed model that uses a dataset or library found to be compromised, or to check a supplier's declared datasets and licences before purchase. Unlike a model card or datasheet, written for people to read, or an experiment log or data version history, which stay with the team that built the model, it is a parts list in a fixed schema that travels with the model and can be matched against vulnerability records and file hashes, but it records what its author declares and verifies none of it.

example_use_cases.description: A bank keeps an ML-BOM for every deployed model, recording each base model by its Hugging Face package URL and revision, the fine-tuning datasets, the framework libraries and the file hashes. When a compromised base-model release or a vulnerability in a model-loading library is announced, its security team queries the BOMs to list the affected deployments within hours and decides which to withdraw or patch.

A hospital trust buying a diagnostic imaging model requires the supplier to deliver a signed ML-BOM with each version. Before the model enters clinical evaluation, the acceptance team checks the BOM's signature, compares its file hashes with the delivered files and checks the listed libraries against known-vulnerability records.

A government department procuring a document-classification model asks bidders for an ML-BOM whose model-card and dataset fields declare each training and evaluation dataset with its source, licence and owner, and the model's known technical limitations. Its assessors and later its auditors read and query these declarations to compare bids and to check what the chosen supplier said it used.

A software company generates an ML-BOM for each release of its customer-support assistant with an open-source generator, recording the base and embedding models, the quantised model file and the framework libraries with hashes. Its security team compares each new BOM with the previous release's to catch an unreviewed change of base model or library before the release ships.

limitations.description: It records what its author declares. Nothing in the format checks that the listed datasets were the ones used, that the model-card fields are true or that the list is complete, so a BOM is evidence that a disclosure was made, not that it is accurate. Hashes and a signature show that the document and the files it lists have not changed since it was written, which is a different thing.

Almost every field is optional: ECMA-424 requires a component's type and name and little else, so a BOM can pass schema validation while saying almost nothing. In a 2026 preprint that generated ML-BOMs with one open-source tool for about 98,000 Hugging Face models, every BOM had the required fields, but only 39% named a dataset, 17% listed technical limitations and 0.2% had a meaningful description. A claim needs the fields it relies on to be checked, not only schema validity.

Generators can fill only what they can read: hub metadata, model-card text and configuration files. Training data, fine-tuning history and settings that the publisher never wrote down stay empty, and for a model bought from a supplier the BOM is only as complete as the supplier chooses to make it.

Each BOM describes one version of one model. Fine-tuning, quantisation, a new framework release or a changed dataset needs a new BOM, and the ability to answer 'which of our models use this component?' when a compromise is disclosed depends on BOMs being regenerated and kept for every deployed version, which is a standing process cost rather than a one-off task.

techniques.name: Human Rights, Democracy and the Rule of Law Risk and Impact Assessment
techniques.description: HUDERIA is the Council of Europe's methodology for identifying and assessing the risks an AI system poses to human rights, democracy and the rule of law, and for planning how to prevent or reduce them, from design through deployment to retirement. It is non-binding guidance that public and private organisations may use or adapt in whole or in part; it was drawn up to support risk assessment in line with the Council of Europe's Framework Convention on Artificial Intelligence, and the human rights treaties its resources cite are illustrative, binding only the states that are parties to them. A multidisciplinary team first runs a context-based risk analysis (COBRA): it scopes the system's purpose, data and affected groups, works through risk factors in the system's application, design and deployment contexts, maps potential impacts on specific rights and on democratic and legal processes, gives each impact an initial rating, and triages the system, deciding whether further assessment is needed and whether the system should be built or deployed at all. Impacts are rated for severity, judged by scale (how serious the harm is), scope (how many people, which groups and for how long) and reversibility (whether those affected can be restored to their earlier position), and for probability; for systems that may pose significant risks, the team may engage affected stakeholders and then re-examines and re-rates each impact in a fuller risk and impact assessment. The output is a mitigation plan that prefers avoiding a harm to reducing, repairing or compensating for it, names who is responsible for each measure, outlines where appropriate the remedies open to affected people, and schedules repeat reviews as the system and its context change.

example_use_cases.description: A city council's children's services department is offered a model that ranks safeguarding referrals for follow-up. A team of caseworkers, a data scientist and a human rights lawyer runs the context-based risk analysis, maps impacts on family life, non-discrimination and fair procedure, and at triage asks whether existing caseworker screening would serve the problem better and whether the referral data represent the families concerned, before deciding whether to procure the model at all.

A recruitment software company assessing a CV-screening model engages disabled and older job seekers, the groups its analysis found most exposed, then rates each mapped impact for scale, scope, reversibility and probability under a scoring rule it writes down. Its mitigation plan drops a feature that scored video interviews, an 'avoid' measure, rather than relying on correcting decisions afterwards, and names the owner of each remaining measure.

A national tax authority that assessed its fraud-risk model before launch repeats the risk and impact assessment when it adds bank-transaction data, and again when a change in benefit rules alters who is flagged. Each review updates the mitigation plan and the information and appeal routes offered to people wrongly flagged, so the assessment on file describes the system as it now runs.

A health ministry outside Europe adapts HUDERIA for a symptom-checker chatbot, keeping the treaty references in the risk-factor and impact lists only for the instruments its state is party to and adding its own constitution, health law and data protection law, while keeping the four elements and the severity variables so that its assessments follow a published structure others can recognise and check.

limitations.description: HUDERIA leaves the rule for combining scale, scope, reversibility and probability into a risk level, and the thresholds used at triage, to the authorities or project teams applying it. Two teams can rate the same system differently and both be following the methodology, so an assessment can be compared or checked only if the team records the scoring rule it chose and why.

Stakeholder engagement and the detailed risk and impact assessment are optional, and are expected mainly for systems that the team's own triage finds may pose significant risks. A team that under-rates a system at triage can skip the stages most likely to expose the problem, so the evidence is stronger when someone outside the team has reviewed the triage reasoning.

The assessment rests on documents, expert judgement and what stakeholders report; it does not test the system. Probability ratings made before a system is built can be little more than informed estimates, so claims about how the system actually behaves, for example whether it treats groups differently, need test results from other techniques alongside the assessment.

HUDERIA assesses one system at a time. It asks teams to consider cumulative effects when a system runs alongside others serving similar purposes, which is where many harms to democratic and legal processes arise, but gives no method for estimating them. An assessment can therefore find each system acceptable while their combined contribution to a wider harm goes unmeasured, so claims about societal impact need evidence beyond a single assessment.

A full assessment needs people who can judge impacts on rights in law as well as people who understand the system's data and design, and it is meant to be repeated over the system's life. Organisations without access to human rights legal expertise may be unable to carry out the impact mapping and mitigation planning to the depth the methodology intends.

techniques.name: AI Incident Reporting with the OECD Common Reporting Framework
techniques.description: AI incident reporting with the OECD common reporting framework records each event in which an AI system caused harm, or could plausibly have caused it, in the common set of 29 fields the OECD published in February 2025, so that reports from different organisations, sectors and countries can be compared and pooled. The framework is meant for both mandatory and voluntary reporting and defines what a report contains, not the reporting interface or what should happen afterwards. The reporter first classifies the event using the OECD's definitions: an AI incident is an event in which the development, use or malfunction of an AI system directly or indirectly leads to harm to people's health, disruption of critical infrastructure, a violation of human rights or of laws protecting fundamental, labour or intellectual property rights, or harm to property, communities or the environment, and an AI hazard is one that could plausibly lead to such harm. Seven fields are mandatory: a title, a description, how the AI system was involved (as a direct cause, a contributing factor, a failure to act, through over-reliance or misuse, through human error, or through a failure to comply with the law), who is reporting, supporting material, the severity (hazard, serious hazard, incident, serious incident or disaster) and the type of harm. The other 22 record, where known and among other things, when and where it happened, the system and the organisations behind it, the people affected, the sector, how widely the system was deployed, whether training data, the model or several interacting systems were involved, the system's task and level of autonomy, and any action taken, giving an inspectable register of what went wrong in operation.

example_use_cases.description: A retail bank's model risk team logs every complaint from customers or staff about its credit, fraud and customer-chatbot models that meets the OECD definition of an AI incident or hazard. A wrongly refused loan, an account frozen by a fraud alert and a chatbot quoting the wrong fees are recorded on the same severity scale and harm types, with the model and version and how the model was involved, so the quarterly risk committee can see which systems recur and which harms dominate.

A hospital records near misses as well as harms. When a radiologist notices that the imaging triage model has put an urgent scan at the back of the queue, the event is logged as an AI hazard, with the model's erroneous ranking as a direct cause, its autonomy recorded as human-in-the-loop, and the action taken, so that patterns of near misses are visible before one becomes an incident.

A national regulator that receives AI incident reports from deployers in several sectors asks for them in the OECD format, with a published note on how it judges seriousness, so that it can count serious incidents by sector and harm type and compare its figures with those of other authorities using the same fields.

A city transport authority running an AI traffic-signal optimiser records a period of emergency-vehicle delays as an incident affecting critical infrastructure, with the system as a contributing factor and an operator's configuration change as human error, so the record shows both causes and the follow-up actions assigned to the supplier and to its own staff.

limitations.description: A register is only as complete as the reports that reach it. Harms nobody notices, such as people quietly refused a service, and events staff have reasons not to report go unrecorded, so a short register is weak evidence that a system has caused little harm unless the organisation can also show how incidents are detected and how reporting is encouraged.

The OECD's own definitions say that seriousness is highly context-dependent, that each jurisdiction may define it differently, and that several small incidents can add up to a serious one. Two reporters can classify the same event differently, so counts of serious incidents can be compared only between reporters that share a written severity rule.

The framework standardises what is recorded, not how an incident is investigated or fixed, and the OECD paper explicitly gives no guidance on corrective or preventive action. Its field for how the AI system was involved is a short category list, and the fields on training data and the model are optional free text, so an organisation needs its own root-cause and follow-up process if records are to lead to changes.

None of the seven mandatory fields identifies the system or its version, the organisation that deployed it or the date of the event. Records kept to the mandatory minimum cannot trace incidents to a model release or show repeated failures of one system; the framework lets a reporting scheme make more fields mandatory, and an organisation that needs this traceability has to do so.

The framework is a recent proposal that the OECD planned to test through open submissions to its AI Incidents Monitor. Regulators that impose a legal duty to report incidents set their own format, categories and deadlines, so an organisation under such a duty reports in the regulator's format, may need to keep the OECD fields alongside, and cannot assume that an event serious on the OECD scale meets the legal definition of a serious incident, or the reverse.
